Senator Tim Scott joins anchor John Roberts to break down the battle for Senate control as the midterm elections approach. They analyze the latest power rankings, key toss-up races, and top economic issues like the cost of living. Scott discusses Republican strategies to win the majority with nineteen days left before voters head to the polls.

With an 8-point lead on the generic congressional ballot — among their highest of the cycle — Democrats could well be on the cusp of a major wave election.

We say this based on historical trends and the current political mood. At this point in 2018, the last blue wave, Democrats led the generic ballot by roughly 7 points before gaining 41 House seats.

Moreover, the president’s party losing seats in midterms is essentially law in American politics: It has happened in all but three elections since the Roosevelt administration.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG?

From 1934 through 2018, the president’s party lost an average of 28 House seats and four Senate seats, and over the past five midterms, the average net loss for the president’s party has been 31 House seats.

To be clear, Republicans could make up ground for a number of critical reasons: Democrats remain divided ideologically, lack a message and an identity other than being anti-President Trump, and Republicans have a considerable cash advantage.

DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS

That being said, by most measures, Democrats have the upper hand in the House and a genuine opportunity in the Senate.

Recent polling suggests Democratic strength in several key Senate battlegrounds — enough to put the upper chamber in play in what was supposed to be a GOP-friendly map.

DEMOCRATS ARE WITHIN STRIKING DISTANCE IN THE SENATE, BUT SHOULDN'T CELEBRATE YET

In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by nearly 10 points in the polling average.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed holds a narrow 3-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers, who had led during the spring and part of the summer as Republicans emphasized El-Sayed’s socialist lean, controversial statements, and his association with far-left influencer Hasan Piker.

EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY

In Maine, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson holds a slight edge over Republican Sen. Susan Collins, although the race remains effectively a toss-up per RealClearPolitics.

Victories in those three states alone would not give Democrats control of the Senate. They need a net gain of four seats.

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL

The deeper problem for Republicans is that Democrats have expanded the map.

In Texas, which has not elected a Democrat statewide since 1994, James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton — President Trump’s preferred candidate — by roughly 3 points.

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

Races in other reliably Republican states, including Iowa, South Carolina, Alaska, and even Kansas — which has not elected a Democratic senator in nine decades — also show Democratic candidates running far more competitively than expected.

The Democratic Party’s weak brand — exacerbated by the growing influence of socialists and the far left — could alienate moderate voters, an argument Republicans are now making. Further, with an average approval rating of 40%, the Democratic Party is virtually as unpopular as President Trump.

Most of these polls remain within the margin of error. But that should offer Republicans little comfort: The fact that these races are close at all reflects a national environment currently favoring Democrats.

That is not to predict that Democrats will win all, or even most, of these contests.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Outside North Carolina, their leads are essentially ties, and polling has underestimated Republican support in several recent elections.

The generic ballot also cannot be applied mechanically to an individual Senate race or House district, particularly when the number of competitive districts has declined sharply since 2018.

The Cook Political Report currently rates 21 House races as toss-ups and another 21 as leaning toward one party or the other. In 2018, 75 races were considered competitive — a decline driven by redistricting and growing political polarization.

Even with those caveats, Democratic competitiveness in traditionally Republican territory is significant in its own right.

DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT

It reflects voters’ deep frustration with the state of the economy. In Fox News polling, nearly four times as many Americans said they were falling behind financially as said they were getting ahead, 44% to 12%.

Fox also found that 55% believed Democrats would do a better job handling inflation, compared with 40% who chose Republicans.

President Trump’s approval rating, meanwhile, is below 40% — another warning sign.

Low presidential approval has often produced punishing midterms. In 2010, when President Barack Obama’s approval stood at a still-weak 44%, Democrats lost 63 House seats and six Senate seats.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Nevertheless, Republicans retain important advantages.

They have only just begun deploying their substantial cash advantage. The Democratic Party’s weak brand — exacerbated by the growing influence of socialists and the far left — could alienate moderate voters, an argument Republicans are now making.

Further, with an average approval rating of 40%, the Democratic Party is virtually as unpopular as Trump.

It is also possible that lower-propensity Republican voters heed Trump’s call to behave as if he were on the ballot and turn out. If they do, the election results could look markedly different from today’s polling.

Ultimately, both history and current data favor Democrats. They are likely to win the House and have a better-than-even chance of capturing the Senate. They are competitive in states that would ordinarily be out of reach and are running strongly across the core battlegrounds.

But with three weeks remaining, a Democratic sweep is far from a foregone conclusion. Republicans still have structural advantages and Trump’s unparalleled ability to mobilize his base.

The direction of the race is clear; the scale of the outcome is not.

WELCOME TO HOW I Spend My Money, a series on The Journal that looks at how people in Ireland really handle their finances.

Are you a spender, a saver or a splurger? We’re asking readers to keep a record of how much they earn, what they save if anything, and what they’re spending their money on over the course of one week. If you’re interested, send a mail to money@thejournal.ie. We would love to hear from you.

Each money diary is submitted by readers just like you. When reading and commenting, bear in mind that their situation will not be relatable for everyone, it is simply an account of a week in their shoes, so let’s be kind.

Last time around, we heard from a technical program manager on €85K living in Dublin. This week, a civil servant on €95K living in the Midlands.

I’m a 33-year-old accountant working in the civil service. I live in the Midlands with my wife and our six-month-old baby. Financially, at the moment, we are trying to rebuild our savings after a few very expensive years in which we finished a house build, got married and had our first child. I put €550 a month into savings, but regularly, I will have to dip into this amount for certain annual expenses and any unexpected costs that crop up.

My wife is still on maternity leave so we don’t have any ongoing childcare costs yet, but this will likely change in the near future when she goes back to work. We are fortunate to have good jobs that pay well, but over the past year, we have really noticed the increase in all of our bills. Groceries especially seem to have increased a lot and our money in general just doesn’t go near as far as it used to.

In my spare time, I love to stay active. I try and go to the gym or run three times a week and golf once a week. It’s the GAA club championship season now, and I like to get down to see my local club’s matches when I can. I finished playing the sport two years ago, but still like to see how the lads are getting on.

Occupation: Civil servant

Age: 33

Location: Midlands

Salary: €95,500

Monthly pay (net): €4,371 after pension contributions

Mortgage: €1,099

Transport: €85 (charging two EVs, mostly charged at home)

TV and broadband: €140

Bins: €32

Electricity bill: €220 (approx – it varies depending on time of year)

Phone bill: €30 (two mobile phones)

Health insurance: €84 (policy for myself, wife and baby)

Groceries and household items: €800

Subscriptions: €52 (Netflix, Apple Music, Apple Cloud Storage)

Other miscellaneous expenses: €100

Car loan repayment: €452

Road tolls: €100

Gym membership: €85

Other subscriptions: €22

Car insurance: €390

Car tax: €120

Golf membership: €1,500

***

6.50am: Our baby is awake and wants to start the day, so I get up and take him downstairs while my wife gets some more sleep. I give him a bottle and play with him for an hour or so and have my own breakfast of scrambled eggs on toast and a coffee. It’s then time to try and get the little man off to sleep for a nap before I start work. I am working from home today and will clock in around 9am.

9.00am: Success! Baby is down for a nap. My wife takes over the child duties and I clock into work. I check my calendar and I have no meetings today, just what you want to see on a Monday. I have a couple of tasks from Friday that need to be done first, so I get stuck into them.

1.00pm: The morning goes by fairly quickly and the lack of meetings has allowed me to plan out my work for the rest of the week, as well as get all my own tasks done. Time for lunch now. The fridge is fairly bare as we get our shopping delivered on a Tuesday, so it’s slim pickings today. I opt to go to the local shop for a roll. It costs €5.90.

1.30pm: Back to work. The pace of work slows a bit, but I get enough done to feel like I’ve accomplished something today.

4.30pm: Finish work for the day. I head to the kitchen to plan out the dinner for this evening. We have prawns and a load of bits of vegetables from throughout the week, so I decide I’ll make a prawn stir-fry with some peppers, onions and carrots and rice with it. I take some time to complete our online groceries order for tomorrow, adding any items we are low on in the fridge and pantry.

5.30pm: My wife gives our baby a bottle while I get the dinner ready. Once he’s fed and happy, we sit down to eat our stir-fry.

6.30pm: I get dinner cleaned up and the house in order while my wife gives the baby a bath and gets him ready for bed. I also take some time to get my clothes ready for work tomorrow. Tuesday is my anchor day in the office, so I have to be somewhat presentable. Then I put the car on charge, so I have a full battery for the commute in the morning.

9.30pm: Baby asleep, we sit down with a cup of tea and a bowl of cereal to watch The Traitors Ireland, our favourite show on TV at the moment.

10.30pm: Time for bed.

Today’s total: €5.90

7.00am: Wake up and get straight into the shower. I’m tired this morning as we were both up a couple of times during the night with a teething baby, such is life at the moment! I get dressed and am out the door by 7.30am. I drive to the office as we have free parking.

8.30am: I pull into a service station on the motorway to get something to eat. Overnight oats and a cappuccino, my usual order on the way to the office. €9.55 in total.

9.30am: I arrive at work. The commute is long, but thankfully I only have to do it once a week. I head up to my desk on the second floor. It’s an open-plan office, so the rest of the team are all sitting around me. I clock in and catch up with the rest of the team.

11.00am: Myself and a few of my colleagues head to the coffee shop next door to the office for a coffee. I get a cappuccino. (€4.10)

11.30am: Back to work. I have a meeting with my manager to go through the progress of some projects we have on.

1.00pm: Lunchtime. I head to a new café that one of my colleagues recommended. I get a chicken ranch sandwich and a bottle of water. The sandwich was worth the hype, I’ll definitely be back. The price came to €14.25. I check my online banking and see that our grocery shopping payment has been taken (€105.85). This is fairly typical for a normal week. I will still need to go to the butcher’s to get our meat and chicken for the week.

1.45pm: Back to work. I have a few things to close off before the end of the day, so I get stuck into them.

4.00pm: I clock out and make a dash for the car. I like to get out of the city as soon as I can to beat the traffic. I’m on the road in 10 minutes, traffic is moving but still slow enough.

6.00pm: I arrive home starving, but thankfully my wife has dinner made. Homemade chicken curry. We sit down and tuck into it, then it’s time to get the little man off to bed. I’m on bedtime duties tonight so I take him upstairs and get him ready for bed.

9.00pm: Baby is asleep, and it’s time to wind down. I make two cups of tea and we sit down to watch the news and The Traitors Ireland. Another great episode.

10.45pm: Time for bed.

Today’s total: €133.75

8.50am: Wake up wrecked. We had a rough night with the baby. Both of us were up with him for a couple of hours during the night. My wife is on the early shift this morning, letting me get a bit more sleep before work. I crawl out of the bed and get dressed. Thankfully, it’s a work-from-home day today. I head to the kitchen and make the quickest scrambled egg and toast ever and take it into the office with me.

9.15am: I clock into work and go through my emails while eating my breakfast at my desk. I have a few emails to respond to from yesterday evening, so I do them first before making a to-do list for the day.

11.00am: Coffee is needed!! I head to the kitchen and make a coffee and have a banana while I’m on the phone. I’ve saved a beauty product my wife has been looking at. It’s her birthday later this month, so I decide to buy it. I move money from savings to my current account to pay for it. €189 in total.

11.15am: Back to work. I have a call after lunch, so I get my notes prepared for it.

1.00pm: Lunchtime. I head to the kitchen. My wife is away into town with the baby, so I whip something up for myself. I defrost some tomato sauce from last week and cook some pasta to go with it.

1.30pm: Back to work. My call is at 2pm, so I do some last-minute preparation for it before I log into it. It’ll be a long one, expect to be on the call for a couple of hours.

4.00pm: Call finished. It went well, but I’m tired talking. I finish up and clock out around 4.30pm, another work day done.

4.45pm: I head to the gym. I’m lucky that my gym is only five minutes from my house so I’m able to get in and get my workout started before 5pm. Really needed this workout today just to clear the head. I finish up the session before 6pm and head home. I stop at the pharmacy on the way home to pick up my monthly prescription and some infant Calpol. (€25.30)

6.30pm: I’m home and it’s dinner time. Thankfully we had taken some leftover bolognese from last week out of the freezer last night to defrost. I cook some spaghetti, heat the bolognese and we have dinner ready to go in 15 minutes.

7.00pm: I’m on baby duties now while my wife cleans up after dinner. I take the little man upstairs for a bath and get him ready for bed.

8.30pm: Time to wind down, we watch some TV and have a cup of tea. No Traitors episode on tonight so we head to bed a bit earlier.

10.00pm: Time for bed.

Today’s total: €214.30

7.05am: Wake up. Baby has slept through the night and we both feel refreshed. Getting a full night’s sleep at the moment is an amazing feeling. I’m on the early baby duties this morning. I take the little man downstairs for his bottle and a bit of playtime. I have my own breakfast too, overnight oats with some fruit and a coffee. It’s a work-from-home day today again so I get the baby off for his first before I clock into work.

9.00am: Clock into work. We have an online training course to complete this morning at 9.30am. It’s fairly boring if I’m honest, but it has to be done. There’s a quiz at the end of each section, so I have to pay attention. The course lasts an hour and a half and I manage to pass all the quizzes.

11.00am: I head to the kitchen and make myself a cup of tea and have a wee scroll on my phone.

11.20am: Back to work. I try to clear off a few things from the to-do list before lunch.

1.00pm: I quickly get changed and head to the gym. I often use my lunch break to get a quick session in when the week is busy. This is the real benefit of having a gym close to the house.

1.45pm: I get back home, quick shower and change. I head to the kitchen and make a sandwich for lunch and bring it with me to the office.

2.00pm: Clock back into work for a call with some of my team. It’s an informal call just to catch up on things, so no prep needed for it.

4.40pm: Another work day done! I clock out and head down to the local butcher’s to pick up some meat and chicken. I pick up our usual bits, chicken breasts, beef mince, steak pieces and a couple of ready-to-cook beef stir-fries. (€33)

5.45pm: I take over the baby-minding duties as my wife goes to a gym class on a Thursday evening. It will be bedtime for the little man soon so let him play on his playmat while I get a bottle and other things ready for him.

7.00pm: I give the baby his bottle and get him into bed. He takes a little longer to settle tonight, but we get there in the end.

7.30pm: My wife comes home from her class and I get started on dinner. I use a ready-to-cook stir-fry that I bought earlier for handiness. I put on some rice to go with it, and we have dinner ready to go in 15 minutes.

8.30pm: Time to wind down for the night. We watch some TV before heading up to bed.

10.30pm: Bedtime.

Today’s total: €33.00

6.15am: Wake up. I do a fitness class in the gym every Friday at 7am so I get up, get the gear on and get some breakfast into me before I head out the door for the class. Overnight oats and fruit for breakfast.

8.15am: Back home after the fitness class, and I am shattered! It was a really tough class. I enjoy getting at least one group class done a week as I reckon I work harder in the group environment than I do when I’m in the gym by myself. I head for a shower and make a coffee before clocking into work.

8.45am: Clocked into work. It’s a work-from-home day again. No meetings or calls in my calendar for today, which is nice. I get going on a few tasks which I’d like to have closed off before the end of the week.

10.50am: I’m starving. I’m always hungrier on the days I go to the gym in the morning. I go to the kitchen and grab another coffee and a Square cereal bar to keep me going until lunch.

1.00pm: I have a haircut booked for my lunch break, so I drive into town to my barbers. He has me in and out in 30 minutes and the cost is €25.

1.45pm: I make a quick sandwich (chicken and salad) for my lunch and take it to my office as I need to clock back in.

2.00pm: I clock back into work. I have a few days of annual leave booked off next week, so I want to finish off a couple of things before I take the days off so I get stuck into them.

4.30pm: All tasks complete, so I clock out for the weekend.

5.30pm: It’s a nice evening so we go for a quick walk with the baby.

7.00pm: Baby’s bedtime. My wife is on bedtime duties tonight so she takes him up to his bedroom. It’s Friday, and it’s takeaway night, so I get our order phoned in and head into town to pick it up. We decided to get a chipper this week: fresh cod and chips for me and cheeseburger and chips for my wife and a side of onion rings to share. (€23.65)

8.00pm: I’m back with the food and the baby is asleep, time to get everything onto plates and tuck in! We crack open a couple of cans of coke to go with the takeaway and get ourselves comfy in front of the TV. We try our best to eat well during the week so we can really enjoy a takeaway at the end of the week.

11.00pm: Time for bed.

Today’s total: €48.65

7.20am: Wake up. Not a great night’s sleep. The little man was up a couple of times during the night, the teething continues. I’m sure other parents of very young children can relate to this unpredictable sleeping. Thankfully it’s the weekend and there’s no work today so we bring the little man into the bed with us and relax for a bit.

8.30am: We get ourselves up and go downstairs. I make us some poached eggs on toast for breakfast and a coffee each. We like to take it easier on the weekends. My local club is playing today in the club championship at 2pm, so I go online and get two tickets (€30 in total). It’s a nice day, so the three of us are going to go to the match. We spend the rest of the morning relaxing and playing with the little man on the floor.

1.00pm: We get the car packed up and head off to the game. The pitch is only 20 minutes away, but we want to get there early so we can get into the stand. We get there around 1.20pm and get great seats on the halfway line.

2.30pm: It’s half-time in the match. My team are losing by a point, but there’s a wind that we will have in the second half, so I’m still hopeful. I go to the shop and get us two coffees. (€9)

3.20pm: Match is over – and we’ve won! Tight game all the way through, but we managed to win by three points in the end and are through to the next round. Time to get back home. Traffic getting out after these games is always hectic so we race to the car to try and get ahead of it.

4.00pm: We get back home. The baby has slept in the car on the way home, which is a great help. My wife’s American relatives are in Ireland at the moment and all her family are heading out to dinner with them tonight, so she starts to get herself ready for the meal. I’m going to stay home and mind the baby, we just want to keep him in a good routine at the moment and keep his bedtime fairly consistent.

6.00pm: My wife heads off with her family into town for the meal. I can’t be bothered cooking now, so I order a Domino’s Pizza and get it delivered (€25). I eat my pizza and scroll on my phone for a while before it’s time to do bedtime with the little man.

7.00pm: I take the little man upstairs for a bath and get him ready for bed. He must be tired after the day out at the game today because he goes straight off to sleep after his bottle. Success!! I head back downstairs with the baby monitor and watch some TV.

9.30pm: My wife is back from the meal. We have a cup of tea together, and I hear all the craic from the night.

10.30pm: Time for bed. I’m up early for golf in the morning.

Today’s total: €64.00

6.00am: Wake up. I like to golf early in the morning to get it out of the way, so I still have most of the day to do other things. I grab a quick bowl of cereal and head out the door at 6.15am. My tee time is 7.20am, but I want to get there a little early to warm up.

6.30am: I get to the golf club and head into the pro shop to check in. It’s a competition day, so it’s €7.50 to enter the competition. I pay my fee and head to the range to warm up.

11.15am: I finish my round. I haven’t been playing well this year, but had a decent round that I could be happy with this morning. I pick up a coffee from the restaurant after my round. (€3.90)

11.40am: I get home – time to unload the car of the golf clubs and load it back up with a child’s buggy. We are heading out to my parents’ house this afternoon to see them. We get all packed up and ready to go and get on the road by 12.30pm.

1.00pm: My parents only live 30 minutes away so we get there by 1pm. We are lucky to have family close by, and we try and visit them most weekends. My mum has lunch made for us all so we sit down and have something to eat and catch up on the craic. We hang around after lunch for a few hours and let my parents look after the baby.

5.00pm: We arrive home after the afternoon in my parents’. It’s nice to be able to go out to their house and relax for a few hours and get some lunch handed to us.

7.00pm: Time to get the little man ready for bed. I give him a bath and my wife gives him a bottle and gets him off to sleep.

8.00pm: We’re both not very hungry after the big lunch we had, so we just make some beans on toast and a cup of tea for our dinner. Then we wind down in front of the TV to end the week.

10.30pm: Time for bed.

Today’s total: €11.40

President of France Emmanuel Macron. File.
                                          | Photo Credit: Reuters

French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday (October 18, 2026) voiced the public's “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 1,800 people have been arrested.

“Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Mr. Macron said in a televised address to the nation.

He blamed “unrestrained violence” on “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”

Mr. Macron has earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with Mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.

Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.

Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday (October 18, 2026) at the Place de la République in Paris amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighbourhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.

“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses in cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.

About 5,50,000 people took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organisers put the figure at about 8,00,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labour union, student organisations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.

Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday (October 18, 2026) approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.

One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor's office said it was investigating.

Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday (October 18, 2026). Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.

Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. The city's prosecutor's office said 557 remained in police custody.

“I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.

Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square's central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.

Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home.

“I was very scared,” he said. “I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.”

Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn't think it would escalate like this.”

“It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement,” she said.

Political leaders across the spectrum sought to parlay the fallout of Saturday's (October 17, 2026) riots into political capital, looking ahead to next spring's presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron's centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted Sunday on social media.

Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, for his part, accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions.”

Mr. Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.”

U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.”

“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote.

French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and other people who joined to loot.

My great-great-grandfather was the namesake of an infamous institution for the disabled. From long-neglected records of the property, the lives of forgotten people were uncovered.

On the Fernald campus. From left to right: Walter Jr, Walter Sr., Tom (the eventual father of Barbara and Winton), Helen (my great-grandmother), and Katherine.

There is a single name across the front of my family gravestone: FERNALD. A simple slab tucked beneath a low-hanging spruce, it would be easy to miss among the grand monuments and lush gardens surrounding it at Mount Auburn Cemetery in Cambridge, Massachusetts. But for many people in the state, the name it bears can still incite a shiver of terror. It was once invoked by teachers and parents as a threat to misbehaving children: “Keep it up and I’ll send you to the Fernald.”

The Walter E. Fernald State School and Hospital, known to locals as the Fernald, sits on a hill in Waltham, Massachusetts, a few miles down the road from my family’s plot. Now an abandoned heap of earth and brick, from its founding in 1848 until its closure in 2014, the Fernald was the oldest institution for intellectually and developmentally disabled people in the Western Hemisphere. For decades, thousands of disabled, neglected, or “behaviorally troubled” children were brought there; many never left. In the mid-20th century, it became one of the nation’s most infamous institutions after journalists, activists, and lawyers brought to light the squalid conditions inside the Fernald, its neglect of patients, and even the medical experimentation, sponsored by corporations like Quaker Oats, that took place there.

In the spring of 2024, I stood before the family stone as my grandma was being buried. She had died a year earlier, and her name was being added to a long list on the back of the stone which began with that of our patriarch: “Walter E. Fernald.” For 37 years, he was the superintendent of the institution that was then called the Massachusetts School for Idiotic and Feeble-Minded Youth. When he died, 100 years before his granddaughter did, flags flew at half-mast across the state, The Boston Globe wrote that his life inspired “something approaching to awe,” and the institution he had run took his name—an honor that ultimately cemented his dishonor.

My grandma had been the family archivist: Cabinets in her home office overflowed with yellowed newspaper clippings and family trees printed from her 1992 Macintosh. I never paid much attention when she extolled our Mayflower origins or showed me photographs of scowling ladies who were apparently related to me. But in September 2022, early in my senior year of college, while I was mapping out a thesis about my older brother’s hospitalizations with a brain illness, I remembered the occasional conversations I had had with her about her famous grandfather. A quick Google search sent a shock of shame up my spine—there were a slew of stories about abuse at the institution he had once run, but also damning information about the man himself. He was labeled a “eugenicist,” a “sterilizer,” a “monster.”

This revelation led me to drive up to my grandma’s nursing home in Northampton, Massachusetts, to ask her about him. Her health was declining at this point, but she was adamant that I had it all wrong: Walter Fernald was not a monster; he was a remarkable man who would visit every single resident each night before bedtime and taught service to others  above all. She insisted that there were no “horror stories” to tell, no matter how much I “seem to want them.” I kept replaying that last point over in my head as I drove back to campus, past the fast fading leaves. Did I want them?

All I knew was that my obsession with Fernald’s legacy only grew. I was lucky that my grandma was such a fastidious record-keeper. I went through her archives, which had been tossed into bankers boxes and were sitting outside in the barn at her old house, and spoke to local historians, but I was only able to view a few of the tens of thousands of records belonging to Fernald that were held in the state’s archives. I could only access the small number that had the patient names redacted due to a draconian Massachusetts law that restricted access to institutional medical records indefinitely—rather than the standard 50 years as specified in the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA). That meant that the Fernald records from 1848 were treated the same as those from 2014.

What I was able to uncover complicated both the condemnations of Walter Fernald that I found online and my grandma’s unequivocal praise. He was undoubtedly a fierce supporter of what was then a radical idea: that disabled children should be offered treatment and education rather than being abandoned or neglected by their families. Through his work at the institution and in local school districts, he created the foundations of what we now call special education. But while he was opposed to the practice of forcibly sterilizing residents, he promoted eugenicist ideas about their potential criminality and, for a period of his career, called for their lifelong segregation from the surrounding community. These ideas turned his Waltham institution into the archetype for a national state hospital system—hundreds of sister institutions were established from Maine to California that were designed to permanently warehouse the disabled under the guise of “public safety.” This system—now often forgotten, its abandoned institutions the backdrop to haunted houses or misremembered as asylums (which served the mentally ill and typically had short-term, rather than indefinite, stays)—was among the largest public investments in the country from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. At its peak in 1967, it held nearly 200,000 people, very often against their will; Walter Fernald was one of its original masterminds.

I never got to share what I had learned with my grandma. She died a couple months after my visit. Would she have been disappointed by who her grandfather really was? Vindicated? In denial? I only knew she would have been proud of me for trying to understand our family history. Now, as she was being interred beside Walter, I recognized all the names on the back of the stone. I knew the story. I remembered.

But as I stepped back from the gravestone, I felt my foot drop onto stone instead of grass. I looked down and saw I was standing on a barely visible mud-caked slab with a name I didn’t recognize: “Barbara M. Fernald 1921–1935.” I called to my mother, “Ma, who is this?” She came over and together we scraped the mud off with our soles. She didn’t know, perhaps a cousin of my grandmother’s who had died young. What had kept her name off the central stone? Beside Barbara’s stone I noticed an even smaller square with no words on it—a nameless grave.

Who was Barbara? Who lay beneath that bare slab? Soon after my grandmother’s funeral, Alex Green, a fellow researcher I had met through my work, contacted me. Alex, a lecturer in public policy at Harvard University who was then finishing a book about my great-great-grandfather, had commiserated with my struggles with the state’s exceptionally restrictive records law. He had sued the state to get access to records from Fernald that were over 100 years old and, in order to view them, agreed to have his notes checked each day to make sure he wasn’t recording confidential patient information. He was so frustrated by the obfuscation that he persuaded the Legislature to create a Special Commission on State Institutions to study, among other things, the state’s actions with regard to records and offer recommendations for ways to improve access to them. Signed into law in July 2022, the 15-person commission—the nation’s first disability rights-led human rights inquiry into the legacy of institutionalization—met for the first time in June 2023.

“This may be a bit of a shock,” he now told me, “but I am fairly certain Fernald had two grandchildren who died in institutions for children with intellectual disabilities.” He had come across offhand references to them in his research. Tom Fernald, my grandmother’s uncle, had two children who both had PKU, a now-treatable genetic condition that causes toxic buildup of the amino acid phenylalanine and leads to progressive brain damage. Barbara Fernald had died at age 13 at a private facility in Pennsylvania in March 1935. Her younger brother Winton had been admitted to Fernald’s sister school, the Wrentham State School, where he died at age 21 in June of 1946. That was all Alex had.

The private facility in Pennsylvania was long closed, and according to the local historical society, its records had almost certainly been destroyed or lost. But I knew Winton’s records must be out there, in some basement archive, but that the state was not going to give me access to them, even though I was related to him and he was long dead.

This restriction was not only absurd but hypocritical. I knew, despite the state’s supposed emphasis on protecting patients’ identities, that thousands of records from as recent as the 1990s had been left on the abandoned grounds of the Fernald for hordes of trespassers to steal and vandalize. I knew it because I’d seen the documents myself.

A couple months after my grandmother’s death, on a cold January morning in 2023, I sat in a car outside the metal gate leading to abandoned acres of the Fernald. I watched Bryan Parcival, a local photographer and Fernald historian I’d befriended through my research, jostle the gate’s lock. “If this doesn’t work we’ll have to hike on,” he said as he shook and twisted the key. With a sudden crack, the lock opened and fell to the ground. He pushed open the groaning gates and hopped back into the driver’s seat. “I got this key five years ago when the state had me take photos of this place. The guy who gave it to me, some maintenance man, died a few weeks later, so no one knows I have this.” He lifted the little silver key up to my face and smiled. “You ready?” he asked, and without waiting for my reply, he drove us past the “No Trespassing” signs and onto the property no one in my family had set foot on in decades.

I followed Bryan’s footsteps as he darted across the buckling wood floors into the Asylum building, which once served as the institution’s main hospital. Mountains of rusted wheelchairs lay crumpled on their sides beside wooden restraint chairs with thick black ropes. Spilling from cabinets was a stream of papers that lay beside books with broken spines, children’s drawings of butterflies, sheet music for “Ode to Joy,” forks, knives, and spoons. I picked up one of the loose papers, a patient record from 1995 titled “Psychotropic Medical Treatment Plan” with a person’s name, birthday, medications, symptoms, and a diagnosis of “chronic schizophrenia” clearly visible. It was one of thousands like it that dotted the floor.

Of course, the campus was technically off-limits. But in 2020 and 2021, the cameras Bryan had set up around the property recorded more than 5,300 incidents of trespassing, during which buildings were frequently damaged and records were stolen, urinated on, and graffitied. One video showed people shooting pornography in the abandoned library that had once housed one of the largest collections of disability literature in the nation. He shared all of this with the City of Waltham, which has owned the property since the institution’s closure. Nothing happened. A police spokesperson told me that they were unable to secure the property due to its size. Urban explorers shared their adventures openly on social media. A local teenager told me it was a rite of passage for kids in the city to visit the campus and that he personally had multiple boxes of patient records in his room that he had swiped. “Do you want to see them?” he asked.

I wrote an article in early 2024 for The Boston Globe about these blatant violations of both HIPAA and the state’s own more restrictive records law that had taken place with the knowledge of the state and the city. The Massachusetts Department of Developmental Services (DDS) blamed the state’s Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance (DCAMM) for failing to remove the records in 2014. The DCAMM responded by shifting the blame back to the DDS. Meanwhile, Waltham’s mayor stayed mum. The article changed little for the campus itself. Over the past two years, some of its oldest buildings have been destroyed by arson, and the town has opened a park on a corner of the property that includes miniature golf and a train. The state did remove thousands of records from the campus. According to Caitlin Ramos, the curator at the Massachusetts State Archives, they were extremely damaged and were ultimately all destroyed by the DDS.

But the article did have one major effect: People who were desperate to get some information about loved ones who had died at the Fernald began to reach out to me. One had heard that his sister had choked to death on peanut butter while she wasn’t being properly supervised, another wanted to track down a beloved aunt who had vanished during his childhood, and another had recently discovered that he had a cousin he had never been told about, and he wanted to find his unmarked grave and buy a proper headstone. The state had previously rebuffed them all, telling them it was to protect the privacy of the patients. What privacy was there on the moldy floors of the Fernald?

One of those who had been denied access was Susan Ruderman, a 64-year-old fifth-generation Bostonian who had long known that her mother, Betty, had a missing sibling. In January 1933, when Betty was 4, her half-brother didn’t come home after school. “Where’s Larry?” she recalled her older brother asking. Their mother turned to the two children and barked, “Never speak of him again!”

Despite her mother’s admonition, Betty occasionally mentioned her long-lost sibling to her daughter. In 2019, years after Betty’s death, Susan became concerned that she might be a carrier of PKU and decided to track down what happened to the lost boy, whose name was all she had to go by. Combing through the 1940 US Census, she found an entry for Lawrence Barry. He was listed as a resident of the Fernald. A request to the state archives for his records led to a typical bureaucratic response: She was told that she needed to hire a lawyer, go to court to prove lineage, and be appointed guardian of his estate. It was too much; she begrudgingly let Larry slip back into the well of silence where he’d sat for decades.

But in May 2025, the Special Commission on State Institutions that Alex had helped start and which he served as vice chair of, released its final report on the decades of mistreatment and disregard for records and graves at the Fernald and other state institutions. In response, in November of that year, Governor Maura Healey signed a law that opened the state’s institutional records to families and researchers 75 years after their creation or, if still held by the DDS or the Department of Mental Health, 50 years after the death of the patient. Alex estimates that 75 to 100 million formerly hidden records were found, received, and opened to the public and that more than 1,000 people have been able to access the story of their loved ones. (The state archive did not immediately keep track of access to institutional records under the new law, but between July 1 and October 13 of this year, 143 people received records; the vast majority are family members of former patients.) The new law also temporarily paused the destruction of documents, a de facto admission that the state had been destroying them. Massachusetts, once one of the most restrictive states for access to institutional records, overnight became one of the most transparent.

Susan made a new request and received Larry’s records within days. There was no evidence of PKU in Larry’s records, but what they did reveal was that he was admitted to the Fernald in 1933 at the age of 8 as a “neglected child,” and that he was determined to escape. A medical note dated November 17, 1933, a few months after he was brought to the Fernald, indicated that he was constantly getting into fights and sprinting from the campus into the surrounding neighborhoods. According to the records, after he was brought back on one occasion, he said, “[I’m] posted anyway, so what’s the use of being good?” The file documents years of constant escapes from wards, infirmaries, haylofts, and, once, from a bean patch on the school’s farm. He stole bikes, made it to train stations, and was caught by local residents and police in towns near and far. He was continually being brought back. His yearly files often ended with the same two sentences: “He had no visitors and no correspondence. Clothing is free.”

After an escape when he was 18, the institution gave up on tracking him down. The file continues with notes that the Fernald staff occasionally received phone calls reporting that he was in and out of prisons and other institutions. The final accessible record was from January 1951, when a Waltham police officer questioned a suspicious-looking man at the employee residence at the Fernald; the man claimed that he was a sailor from California and thought the place was a hotel. In fact, he was Larry Barry, returning to the place he hated so much that he’d escaped a hundred times but that was also the only home he’d ever known. The unnamed staff member who wrote the note told the police officer that Larry was not a patient anymore and “they were free to deal with him as they saw fit.” Larry was taken away by the police.

While many questions are left unanswered, Susan says this access was an unbelievable gift—an opportunity to finally get a glimpse of a family member who had been relegated to oblivion since that cold January day in 1933. She is determined to find out what happened to him after he was taken by the Waltham police in 1951, to find his grave, and, if necessary, give it a proper stone.

Just as it did for Susan and the dozens of other people who reached out to me for help, the change in the law meant I could access not only Walter Fernald’s records but also those of his grandson. Within a matter of days, I received Winton’s records from the DDS in an e-mail. It included his autopsy report, which gave him a mental age of 2 years and 10 months and a diagnosis of “imbecile,” a series of medical and psychological notes from his admission at the age of 1 to his death 20 years later, and two photos: one at age 7, standing in a field with a mischievous smile on his face, and another at age 20, in an oversize suit with a large white handkerchief protruding awkwardly from the chest pocket, staring grimly down against a black background. The records show that Winton was constantly shredding his clothes and, as he grew older, smashing his fists into windows. He often had to get stitches on his knuckles. He occasionally had visitors, but his parents, perhaps because of the trauma of institutionalizing two of their children, moved to Florida shortly after his birth and apparently rarely visited Massachusetts.

Wrentham was founded and run by one of Walter Fernald’s closest protégés, Dr. George Wallace. It is very likely that this is why Winton was brought there, and perhaps, though the records don’t reflect this, he received special attention because of his last name. But after Wallace’s sudden death in 1930, Wrentham, like most institutions in the period coinciding with the Great Depression and then the Second World War, had scant funding and dangerously few employees. One staff member per 50 residents was common. Whatever special attention he might have had was likely gone—it is no wonder he kept smashing his fist into windows.

In the final pages of his records, I found proof that Winton was indeed buried under that small stone square at the family plot at Mount Auburn. The files have no mention of his grandfather, the man who had bought that plot, whose name had been bestowed on the institution a few miles down the road, and who had helped create the very system of institutionalization in which his grandson had died. No, it just says Winton died with his mother at his bedside, that he was cremated and buried beside his sister, Barbara, laid to rest 10 years earlier. Unlike her, he did not get a name.

These records cannot do much. Written in the institution’s removed hand, they cannot truly tell his experience, what he was like, what he thought or felt or desired. His life was just one drop in a great ocean of forgotten lives. But is that so special? Despite our best attempts to archive the past, to keep the records from rotting, from potter’s fields to Mount Auburn, from institutions to families, isn’t forgetting the one inevitable thing?

But even so, why do I keep looking at the sad photographs of this faraway boy? What do I want from these “horror stories”? Why do I keep reading and rereading the records, especially returning to the rare moments when he speaks? Such as the January 3, 1941, examination in which he kept repeating, “So glad I’m going home” and “I hate this damn dump.” Or on November 12, 1935, when he kept begging the nurse, “Turn light on, Miss. It’s dark, Miss.” The game, the report says, was an “obsession with him and it was practically impossible to get him to stop.” He jumped up and down and up and down, flicking the light on and off and on and off, answering questions at random, until he finally declared, “No more.”

Oliver Egger is a writer and editor based in New Haven, Connecticut.

Two young hikers endured a freezing, 36-hour ordeal on California’s Mount Shasta after losing their way in treacherous terrain, becoming trapped between towering cliffs and running out of phone battery as a frantic rescue played out to find them.

The 19-year-old man and 20-year-old woman, both from Salt Lake City, called for help around 10:20 p.m. Monday, Oct. 12, after becoming too cold and exhausted to safely complete their descent from the 14,179-foot mountain, according to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office.

The pair had planned only a day hike while a friend continued to the summit. But by the time they called for help from the Avalanche Gulch area at roughly 11,000 feet, temperatures had plunged to between 14 and 16 degrees — and they lacked adequate clothing, food and water to safely spend the night.

They had reached Red Banks on the Avalanche Gulch route around 5 p.m. Monday — five hours past the recommended turnaround time for climbers on Mount Shasta, authorities said.

The sheriff’s office thanked search-and-rescue volunteers, Mount Shasta climbing rangers and CHP Air Operations for bringing the hikers to safety.

But officials warned that the rescue was the third of its kind on the Avalanche Gulch route in the past month.

A roof engulfed in flames is seen during the Norte Fire on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, in San Juan Capistrano, Calif.

A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.

Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.

Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.

"Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse," said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.

Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.

Laura Hart hasn't had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she's lived in the community, she said.

"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said. "We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."

The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.

It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.

Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.

The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.

"The fire is right up on the city," said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."

Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.

Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.

Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.

The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.

"You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke," Needham said.

Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 118,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.

The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

LEXINGTON, SC — The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double-murder retrial rebuked both sides Friday over their bitter evidence fights, warning she “will not allow these proceedings to become a circus.”

During the tense hearing, Judge Debra McCaslin handed the defense a win on their DNA testing request but rejected its broader request for ballistic data.

McCaslin also corrected the record on a polygraph claim that Murdaugh attorney Dick Harpootlian made in August, which he said Murdaugh passed with “flying colors.” The judge said Friday that Murdaugh actually failed that test, which was related to his financial crimes, not the murder case.

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family’s Moselle property in Colleton County.

The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury.

His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings.

McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors’ objections on DNA samples of swabs from Maggie Murdaugh’s phone, even though the analysis will likely consume the last testable samples.

She cited due process and the right to a “full and complete defense.” Murdaugh’s defense team said the testing will likely take about 90 days.

The judge said defense attorneys don’t have to share results of the DNA tests with prosecutors unless they plan to use them at trial.

McCaslin denied Murdaugh’s request for a list of every crime in the 2nd and 14th judicial circuits since 2021 involving .300 Blackout ammunition, for every such firearm recovered, and for casings from other shootings.

She found the theory that the murder weapon is tied to an unsolved crime speculative and was based solely on news reports, adding that the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division doesn’t have a list like that, and a manual review would be too much work and could intrude on investigations that are ongoing.

While the judge denied Harpootlian for his expert to physically test the shell casings from the crime scene, she ordered the state to hand over all raw data to the defense.

She also said prosecutors must hand over 3D crime scene scan data by Monday, but added she won’t make the state produce material several times and asked the defense to have staff sign for discovery.

McCaslin issued a similar warning when the state agreed to provide the defense with cellphone extraction data from Maggie and Paul’s phone, but said this would be the last time the state will hand it over.

To close the hearing, McCaslin granted a state motion to correct the record regarding Harpootlian’s assertion at an Aug. 14 hearing that Murdaugh had passed a polygraph “with flying colors.”

She said Murdaugh had been administered a polygraph concerning whether he concealed other assets and failed it, and that he has never taken a polygraph related to the killings of Maggie and Paul Murdaugh.

McCaslin acknowledged that Harpootlian had submitted a letter expressing apology for any confusion, then cautioned both sides that “candor with the court is not optional.”

McCaslin also ruled in prosecutors’ favor on a defense motion requesting evidence related to the disposal of the murder weapons, which have never been recovered.

McCaslin said the state is required to hand over the material only if it proves favorable to Murdaugh’s defense.

Murdaugh’s defense team initially asked the judge to force prosecutors to turn over information it has “concerning the handling, transport, concealment, or disposal of the alleged weapons used to kill Maggie Murdaugh and Paul Murdaugh, including the statement a witness gave to agents of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division in 2023 that a Lowcountry police chief spoke of arriving early at the scene and of providing Defendant Murdaugh a change of clothes, the reports of every interview conducted on that subject, and the testimony and exhibits presented to the State Grand Jury concerning it.”

According to the motion, filed in late September by Murdaugh’s attorneys, press reports indicate that a state grand jury received testimony alleging Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander was observed in possession of the murder weapons shortly after the June 7, 2021, killings.

“According to those reports, witnesses have testified that the Chief of Police of the Town of Yemassee, Greg Alexander, was seen with the murder weapons in the immediate aftermath of the June 7, 2021, killings, and that second Yemassee officer is under investigation for transporting and concealing weapons and clothing,” the filing states.

It cites a story from The Post and Courier, which reported that “a Lowcountry official told SLED agents that Chief Alexander ‘spoke of arriving early to the murder scene and talked about providing a change of clothes to Murdaugh,’ and that the official believed the guns and clothing were brought into the police station and stored there.”

Notably, the allegations couldn’t be corroborated by The Post and Courier.

Alexander, through his attorney, Joe McCulloch, denied accusations made in the media reports.

“The same explanation has been provided to SLED,” McCulloch told Fox News Digital. “That truth will outlive any ridiculous rumors and gossip.”

Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital he considers the allegation against Alexander a “wild goose chase.”

“This is one of those cases that, you know, a lot of reporting was done early on, a lot of conspiracy theories swirling around this case,” Ritter said.

“I don’t see any reason for the judge to allow for this essentially wild goose chase in regards to an uncorroborated report about law enforcement perhaps being in possession of the murder weapon.”

“Obviously, the defense would love to pursue this to its absolute limit because they think that there’s a snowball’s chance that it might yield something, but I think that the judge is probably going to give very little leeway on something like this,” he added.

A deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, left three students and a teacher dead before an armed bystander shot and killed the teenage gunman. Sarah Alegre provides updates from the scene.

Democrats renewed calls for tougher gun laws after three children and a teacher were killed in an Oregon school shooting, but gun-rights advocates say the circumstances of the attack bolster their case against new restrictions.

The teenage shooter reportedly opened fire with a shotgun purchased by his mother before an armed father-of-two-students, Kaylub Giamanco, pursued him into Silver Rail Elementary School and fatally shot him. Second Amendment advocates argue additional gun restrictions would not have stopped the killer and could make it harder for armed civilians like Giamanco to intervene.

"Democrats are shamefully weaponizing this tragedy in Oregon to advance their political agenda on gun control," Aidan Johnston, director of federal affairs for Gun Owners of America, told Fox News Digital.

"But more gun control isn’t the solution. The school was a gun-free zone, and the killer didn’t use a so-called ‘assault weapon.’ What did stop the mass murderer and save lives was an armed bystander with good aim."

School buses are lined up outside Silver Rail Elementary School where there was a shooting Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)

Gun-rights researcher John Lott, president of the Crime Prevention Research Center (CPRC), separately argued that restrictions on carrying guns can leave potential victims defenseless.

"These gun-free zones actually serve as a magnet for these attacks rather than stopping them from occurring," Lott told Fox News Digital.

Lott pointed to CPRC research examining active shootings from 2014 through 2024, which he said found that legally armed civilians stopped more attacks than police did.

The National Rifle Association similarly questioned whether new restrictions would have changed the outcome.

"Oregon already has nearly every gun-control measure on the anti-gun wish list — including an A- rating from groups that push them — yet that did not prevent this attack," the NRA said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"The armed bystander who pursued the shooter inside and ended the threat is the clearest reminder that, when seconds count, a prepared law-abiding citizen can stop a killer."

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., was among the lawmakers calling for action after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where Bend-LaPine school policy bans firearms, including concealed guns.

"The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass commonsense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement.

Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary School after a shooting Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)

Nelson then called Kariem’s wife, Eboni, who was waiting outside the attraction and knew something was wrong but did not yet know what had happened, the outlet reported.

Moments later, Kariem’s wife heard authorities announce that someone had died. She immediately feared the victim was her husband.

The girl was OK after the terrifying incident, her father added.

Consumer prices rose sharply in September.

The consumer price index rose 0.6 percent in September compared with August, driven higher by rising gasoline prices, the Labor Department said Wednesday. Over the year, the consumer price index is up 3.7 percent.

Core prices, a measure that excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September. Compared with a year ago, core prices are up 2.6 percent. That is a decline in year-over-year core inflation from last month’s 2.5 percent.

Economists had forecast CPI would increase by 0.6 percent from the prior month and 3.7 percent from a year ago. Core prices were expected to rise 0.2 percent for the month and 5.2 percent over the past 12 months.

Gas prices rose 9.1 percent in September, which the Labor Department said accounted for over half of the monthly headline increase. The energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August. For the year, energy prices are up 20.4 percent.

There was some good news for consumers in the grocery aisle.  The index for food at home fell 0.1 percent.  Prices for dining out rose 0.2 percent.

Electricity prices rose 0.2 percent in September after falling 0.2 percent in August. This follows a 0.1 percent increase in July and a 1.0 percent decline in June. For the year, electricity is 4.4 percent higher.

Apparel prices rose 0.3 percent in September after being flat in August, rising 0.1 percent in July, and falling 0.6 percent in June. For the year, clothing prices are up 3.4 percent.

Shelter prices rose 0.4 percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August, bringing the yearly gain to 3.2 percent. Rents rose 0.2 percent. Hotel and motel prices jumped 2.0 percent in September after a 2.4 percent rise in August.

Medical care services prices rose 0.3 percent and are up 2.5 percent from a year ago. Medical care goods fell 0.7 percent. These are down 3.3 percent from a year ago. Prescription drug prices declined 1.2 percent for the month after being flat the previous month. They are down 4.5 percent from a year ago. Non-prescription drug prices rose 1.3 percent after falling 1.0 percent the previous month. For the year, they have fallen by 0.9 percent.

Prices of major appliances were unchanged in September after jumping 1.4 percent in August. Compared with a year ago, major appliance prices are down 2.3 percent. Furniture prices fell by 0.8 percent in September after falling 0.9 percent in August. They are down 2.4 percent from a year ago.

Prices of new cars and trucks rose 0.2 percent compared with August. Compared with a year ago, they are up 0.6 percent. Used car and truck prices climbed 0.7 percent after rising 0.4 percent the previous month. Compared with September of last year, however, they are down 1.5 percent.

boebert-small-towns-unique-zip-codes-202:
(Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Rural communities are far too often overlooked in Washington; they deserve a voice in Congress, and their local concerns should be turned into practical law. Postal reform has long been a concern for rural Americans, and ZIP codes are a simple, effective way to address an everyday issue affecting Coloradans.

In Colorado and across rural America, something as simple as a ZIP code can determine whether a community has a clear identity, accurate mail delivery, proper emergency services, and a fair shot at economic growth. For too long, countless small towns have been forced to share ZIP codes with larger neighboring communities, leading to confusion, delays, and a lack of recognition.

That is why I introduced H.R. 3095, the Unique ZIP Code bill. This legislation would direct the Postal Service to create single, unique ZIP codes for scores of communities that have waited far too long for basic recognition.

The Unique ZIP Code bill is personally significant because it underscores the importance of listening to constituents and addressing the problems that matter to everyday Americans. My bill passed the House of Representatives with strong bipartisan support.

The Senate companion, S. 4505, introduced by Senator Joni Ernst (R-IA), advanced out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, led by Chairman Rand Paul (R-KY). I am grateful for the progress and remain focused on getting this bill across the finish line and onto the President’s desk.

This effort brought together a bipartisan group of the Colorado delegation to help Coloradans. Original cosponsors for my legislation included Democrats Brittany Pettersen (CO-07) and Jason Crow (CO-06), along with Republicans Jeff Hurd (CO-03) and Gabe Evans (CO-08). Working across the aisle on practical solutions that strengthen our communities is exactly what Coloradans expect from their representatives.

Unique ZIP codes are not a symbolic gesture. They are tangible changes that improve mail delivery accuracy, help emergency services respond to the right location, strengthen local identity, support businesses in operating and growing, and ensure that tax and census data accurately reflect the communities that actually exist. For the 73 communities included in this legislation, unique ZIP codes are long-overdue practical relief.

I have heard from Coloradans who live this frustration every day. Residents who watch packages go to the wrong place. Local leaders who struggle to market their town when it shares a ZIP code with a larger city. Families who simply want their community recognized for what it is. This bill answers those concerns with a common-sense solution.

Small towns are the backbone of Colorado and our nation as a whole. They deserve the same basic tools and recognition that larger communities take for granted. A unique ZIP code is a simple, common-sense reform that strengthens communities without adding bureaucracy or cost.

Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa successfully led S. 4505 out of committee; now our coalition is seeking every opportunity to get this legislation across the finish line.

And this legislation has garnered support from more than just Colorado’s lawmakers. It is backed in both chambers by a bipartisan coalition of members from 17 states, including California, Connecticut, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Oklahoma, Wisconsin, Wyoming, and more. I will continue to work with my colleagues and Congressional leadership to get this legislation passed and signed into law, so that all local voices continue to be heard.

Lauren Boebert represents Colorado’s 4th District in Congress and serves on the House Committee on Natural Resources and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
