A 26-year-old South Dakota sheriff’s deputy has died after being shot during a confrontation at a Sioux Falls home that also left a suspect wounded.

Minnehaha County Deputy Katherine Frank was critically wounded Friday night when gunfire erupted about 30 minutes after deputies arrived at the home, the Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Office said.

Frank and the suspect were treated at the home before being taken to hospitals.

Frank died Monday, surrounded by family and loved ones, after spending three days in critical condition.

“Deputy Frank’s death is a significant loss to our agency and to the broader law enforcement community in and around Sioux Falls,” the sheriff’s office said. “She served the citizens of Minnehaha County with professionalism, humility, and dedication. Her absence will be felt deeply by all who have had the privilege of working alongside her.”

The suspect, Brandon John Oetken, 39, of Sioux Falls, was charged with three counts of attempted first-degree murder of a law enforcement officer and three counts of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer.

Minnehaha County jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital also list a felony offense of disarming a law enforcement officer. Oetken remained in custody without bond Tuesday morning.

It was not immediately clear whether prosecutors planned to file additional charges following Frank’s death.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff’s office and the Minnehaha County State’s Attorney’s Office for more information about the shooting and the charges against Oetken.

The South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation is handling the shooting investigation at the sheriff’s office’s request.

South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley paid tribute to Frank after her death.

“We mourn the loss of Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Deputy Katherine Frank, who sacrificed everything in the line of duty to keep us safe. Let us never forget her courage and the service of all of our law enforcement officers. Deputy Frank and her family remain in our prayers,” Jackley said in a statement.

Jackley previously said investigators would review the use of force during the encounter, with a public report expected within 30 days.

The shooting was the fifth involving law enforcement officers in South Dakota this year, the attorney general’s office said.

Frank worked at the South Dakota State Penitentiary beginning in September 2022 before joining the sheriff’s office in June 2024.

In her final act of service, Frank became an organ donor, continuing to help others even after her death, the sheriff’s office said.

“Deputy Frank served with dignity and heart,” the sheriff’s office said. “Her service made a meaningful difference, and her impact will remain with us always.”
white-house-media-ban-ruling:
David Folkenflik

WASHINGTON, DC - SEPTEMBER 19: CNN signage on the network's booth in the press area of the White House after journalists with the network were earlier denied entry to the White House grounds, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC.
                
                    
                    Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that President Trump cannot ban news organizations from covering him at the White House because he does not like the nature of their coverage — at least, not until the matter goes to a formal trial.

U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to bar more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated their fundamental free speech in two separate ways as well as their due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights to the U.S. Constitution.

The news organizations sued last month after the Trump administration denied them access. The judge granted a temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 24.

Kelly pointed repeatedly to Trump's own public statements and social media posts to construct his conclusion that Trump was not responding to national security concerns. Instead, he wrote, Trump sought to pressure news outlets to cover him more favorably by stripping them of press credentials to gain access to the White House.

"President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before," Kelly wrote in the opinion.

He later continued, "[T]he ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area — a space open to many of their competitors — thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials."

WASHINGTON, DC - OCTOBER 08: Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico Ted Boutrous leaves the E. Barrett Prettyman United States Court House on October 08, 2026 in Washington, DC.
                
                    
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Theodore J. Boutrous, the noted First Amendment attorney representing the three U.S. news outlets, had argued in court last week that Trump was the best witness his clients could offer for their case — because the president was so blatant about not liking the tenor of their coverage. Late Tuesday, after the release of Kelly's ruling, he hailed the judge's words.

"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement shared with NPR.

"Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers," Boutrous wrote. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."

The White House did not immediately return NPR's requests for comment. Nor did the president speak publicly about the ruling in the first hours after the ruling was released.

Kelly, a Trump appointee, turned aside the U.S. Justice Department's arguments invoking national security concerns and the objections the White House took with their reporting. Trump has said coverage is framed in a way to drag him down and make his Democratic critics look good.

The judge also rejected the department's claims that the court should not weigh in on such matters. Kelly had ruled against the Trump administration during the president's first term in office on a related matter involving efforts to bar then CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta. And Kelly pointed to other precedents that he said must guide his conclusions, even as the Justice Department argued in court they were wrongly decided.

Even so, Kelly took pains to note that he did not utterly dismiss those as valid governmental concerns.

"No one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded," Kelly wrote, "or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed."

Even so, Kelly found that the White House's actions to put the president's words into practice had caused a kind of irreparable harm. Trump was not required to admit the reporters to the White House. Once they were credentialed to do so, under earlier court rulings, those credentials could not be stripped away simply because the president or other administration officials do not like their coverage.

The Justice Department invoked national security only in court filings days after the White House acted against the reporters. And the news outlets were neither given fair warning of what was ahead nor a means to object ahead of time. The White House communications office sent letters expressing concern over accuracy and what it said were national security disclosures days later and gave the journalists several days to respond and appeal.

Kelly wrote that the Justice Department's presentation was inadequate to make a compelling case. And he said that after-the-fact notification did not constitute an adequate process to be warned about consequences and to appeal the punishment.

"It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him," Kelly wrote. And that, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation.

WASHINGTON, DC - SEPTEMBER 19: A CNN sign hangs on the wall behind the broadcast area in the White House briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC.
                
                    
                    Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

The ruling did not, however, address the question of the administration's periodic refusal since the ban to permit CNN's journalists into smaller spaces where the full press corps cannot fit simultaneously, such as Air Force One or the Oval Office.

That has made it impossible for CNN to serve as the designated representative of the video pool.

The pool - made up of CNN and four competitors (ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC) - share costs and logistical obligations to capture video of Trump at every public appearance, even in tightly held locations.

Even after Kelly earlier issued a temporary restraining order compelling the administration to allow the reporters back into the White House, the order was observed unevenly. CNN was periodically blocked by the administration from representing the pool either generally or in tight spaces. In one recent instance, CNN was blocked from accompanying Trump aboard Air Force One on a trip to Tennessee.

The three major U.S. news organizations sued shortly after reporters for the outlets reported their credentials, which give them daily access to the White House, were confiscated.

The administration has waged a multi-front battle against the press, including an early review of the broadcast licenses for ABC's local TV stations that could lead to them being revoked. It also forced news outlets out from the Pentagon when they did not agree to withhold any reports that had not been authorized for release ahead of time. The administration has launched investigations of all major networks — including NPR — except Fox, which is controlled by Rupert Murdoch, the president's ally, and successfully pressured the Republican leaders of Congress to pull back all federal funds for public media.

Last week, the Department of Justice said it was investigating five major television networks - CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News, alleging that they have broken antitrust laws when they decided to stick together after the president banned CNN.

As a private citizen, Trump has sued the New York Times, CNN, the Des Moines Register, the BBC, and Wall Street Journal (also owned by Murdoch). ABC settled a Trump lawsuit ahead of his return to office and CBS settled days before its corporate owner received the green light from Trump's pick as the nation's chief broadcast regulator to sell itself to its new owners, allies of the president.

these-workers-help-train-robots-who-coul:
By

Diaa Hadid

,

Omkar Khandekar

KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica. It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.

It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.

Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."

Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."

India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.

"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P., a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."

Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.

What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole, economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."

But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."

That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.

The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."

He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.

Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.

There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.

Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.

"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."

The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000.

Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.

Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.

For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.

And to amass recordings of humans doing work with their hands for clients who request ecocentric data, Ramaswamy says, they pay hundreds of people across India to undertake domestic jobs, like Sneha Jegadish, a 24-year-old who lives on the edge of town.

Jegadish clipped her smart phone to a headset and began chopping a carrot, her phone recording her every hand movement.

She records herself doing housework for a few hours a day, for about $2.60 an hour, and makes around $120 a month. Jegadish folds clothes, wipes the floor, does the dishes — jobs she was never expected to do growing up, because her mother wanted her to focus on her studies. So when she got this gig a few months ago, "my mother had to show me how to do those jobs," she smiles.

Money or not, it's still drudgery, says Jegadish. One day, she hopes, she'll have a robot to do her housework. "The work we are doing now is going to be done by robots in the future," she says.

That's the same conclusion that 42-year-old textile worker Kannagi Periyasaamy has come to.

At the textile factory, Periyasaamy was folding and packing aprons with a GoPro fastened to her head.

She's one of the few workers who is paid about $2.60 an hour to record herself, and she's been told why. She explains: "We are training them [the robots] on how to package the aprons, how to do a quality check, how to fold the aprons."

Periyasaamy says she's been doing this for the past three months, enough for her to be convinced that someday, a robot will take over her job. When that day comes, she says, "I'm thinking about taking up farming" — the family owns a scrap of land where she could raise cattle. Meanwhile, Periyasaamy thinks of AI robots as her students and says, "I'm proud I can teach it to do a good job."

Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)

Most notably for critics, Trump's Mar-a-Lago home was infamously raised by the FBI as part of an investigation into alleged mishandling of classified documents. That case was closed when Trump again won the presidency in 2024.

"In the Trump administration, unlike the previous administration, we let the facts and the law drive this stuff — so the president and I really don't butt ourselves in the DOJ investigations," Vance said. "We're not trying to micromanage this. We're not trying to tell [Attorney General] Todd Blanche to do one thing or another. We try to let the facts drive this thing."

"So we're gonna let the investigation unfold," he went on before warning: "If, of course, criminal wrongdoing is discovered or potentially fraudulent immigration is uncovered, then obviously there will be legal proceedings to follow that."

Rep. Ilhan Omar dismissed Vice President JD Vance’s claims that the Justice Department is investigating her for alleged immigration and fraud violations, referring to House Republicans' attention to the matter as politically motivated. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"I think we have to let the facts and the law drive this, right? So I don't think you can say because politics might be difficult or politics might be easy, you can't follow the law. You have to actually enforce the law as it exists," he said.

"And to the question of it being unprecedented, I mean, what I'd say is that Ilhan Omar herself is a very unprecedented person," he said.

Rep. Ilham Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)

"We have very rarely had a person in Congress who seems to have such disdain and such rage at the country that gave her a better life," Vance said. "Now, that's not a crime."

"But we're going to see whether she did commit a crime. And if she did, we're obviously going to follow the law," he reiterated.

Vance made the comments after rallying on behalf of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton at the Tyler Pounds Regional Airport in Tyler, Texas, a city about 100 miles east of Dallas.

Paxton is running in a neck-and-neck race with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico just three weeks before Election Day, as Republicans fight desperately to hold control of Congress.

ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Tyler Pounds Regional Airport on Oct. 13, 2026, in Tyler, Texas. Vance is in Texas to campaign for Republican candidates on the November midterm ballot. (Saul Loeb-Pool/Getty Images)

TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID

In a post from her official government X account from just after 1:30 p.m., Omar elaborated further.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said.

"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

China's Han Xu was a star attraction for the Perth Lynx last season, and has joined the Geelong Venom.  (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Opals legend Lauren Jackson has a key leadership role heading into the new WNBL season.

The Tasmania Jewels become the competition's ninth team.

The season tips off on Thursday with the Jewels hosting the Geelong Venom.

Thursday night will mark the start of the second season of the Women's National Basketball League (WNBL) under new, private ownership, with the league hoping to build on some of the gains made.

Last season, crowd figures were up 43 per cent, and broadcast reach 130 per cent, but that did not stop the league making its CEO Jennie Sager redundant, in a restructure it said would bring the men's and women's codes under one umbrella.

Sager later called the decision "genuinely disappointing", arguing that "women's sport leagues are strongest when they have dedicated leadership and a staff that wakes up every day solely focused on driving them forward".

Under the 2026/27 leadership model, retired Opals star Lauren Jackson has a key role as Chief Strategy and Basketball Partnerships Officer, and said she was buoyed by the change the consortium of owners had brought.

"Being privatised has been super important for the league in the way we are growing and going through a new phase," Jackson told ABC Sport.

"It has been a long time coming, but it's very exciting.

"I take a lot of pride in the league and feel very honoured that I get to work in it."

Lauren Jackson is a legend of Australian basketball, and is now helping oversee the WNBL.  (Getty Images)

Now in its 47th edition, the WNBL is the oldest women's professional league in Australia, with Jackson saying she was passionate about giving back to domestic basketball.

"The sport has given me so much," she said.

"My legacy off the court is about getting back and building [the WNBL] to a point in Australia where it is sustainable, where it's providing young women with the opportunities that we really had to work and work hard for."

Jackson referenced the league's most recent collective bargaining agreement (CBA) as evidence of that progress, which awarded players a 104 per cent increase in minimum wages.

"The visibility piece is happening globally [and] the sport is taking off," she said.

Aiding in its aspirations for new audiences, the first game of the WNBL season will feature new franchise the Tasmania Jewels, following the success of 2024 NBL champions the JackJumpers.

Darcee Garbin (left) will captain the Tasmania Jewels in their inaugural WNBL season. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The Jewels will host the Geelong Venom in Hobart, led by Opal Steph Reid.

The league has also been buoyed by the signing of Chinese national team players including Shuyu Yang (Canberra Capitals) and Siyu 'Rainy' Yang (Southside Flyers), while 211-cm Han Xu will return for Geelong, having played for Perth Lynx last season.

"We want to be leaders in the Asia Pacific in particular, so being able to have Chinese representation here, and to be able to have some of the best players in the world who are competing in the WNBA, has been really, really good," Jackson said.

Former rookie of the year Jaz Shelley said she was embracing the prospect of further international competition.

"It's really exciting, it has become a global game; we have some unreal American imports and then we have the Chinese coming in, it's just so cool to have players from all different areas, and for the game to be developing," she told ABC Sport.

This season, Shelley has made the move to join coach Renee Garlepp at the Sydney Flames, whose season will launch against the Flyers.

Manuela Puoch has joined the Canberra Capitals, where she will play alongside her older sister, Nyadiew Puoch.

"She said it'll be intense, it'll be fun, she's next door to me," Manuela Puoch said.

And after after having been drafted by the New York Liberty with the 41st pick in the 2026 WNBA draft, her sights are set on the world's top league.

"[My long-term aspirations] are definitely to go to New York, and just keep developing as a player and a person," she said.

(Photo by Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)

John Boyega has been married for nearly two years without making a public announcement, and now he and his wife are preparing to welcome a baby boy. The actor also revealed that he already has a young stepson, giving fans a rare glimpse into a family life he has largely kept out of the spotlight.

The secret marriage came to light during an interview with The Guardian, published October 4, in which the 34-year-old actor discussed his childhood, personal growth, and involvement in a documentary about his late friend Damilola Taylor.

Boyega wasn’t initially discussing his relationship when the conversation took an unexpected turn. After the interviewer noticed a ring on his left hand, the Star Wars star casually acknowledged that he had been married for “coming up two years now.”

Rather than planning an extravagant celebrity wedding, Boyega and his wife chose an intimate ceremony. He jokingly compared the occasion to a scene from Braveheart, pretending to plant a sword into the ground before dramatically asking, “Will you come with me?”

Although the wedding was small, the details he shared suggest the couple found meaning in keeping things simple.

According to The Guardian, Boyega owns two wedding bands, including a two-toned ring with significant “sentimental” value. Surprisingly, that particular piece of jewelry came from an ordinary shopping trip rather than a luxury jeweler.

“This is the one we decided to pick up spontaneously because I just wanted the ring on my finger, so we went to Walmart to get this,” he explained.

He also remembered the experience fondly, adding, “It was a lovely trip to Walmart. Shout out, Walmart Canoga Park!”

For an actor who has appeared in some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, the spontaneous purchase offered a refreshingly simple detail about his secret marriage. The importance of the ring had little to do with its price and everything to do with what it represented.

Despite his Nigerian heritage, Boyega confirmed that the couple did not have a traditional Nigerian wedding ceremony. However, he hasn’t ruled out celebrating their marriage with a much larger gathering in the future.

“We both like the idea of celebrating something established, rather than celebrating the entry,” he explained.

And when that celebration finally happens, Boyega joked that it could become an unforgettable occasion.

“And by then, we’ll have to shut Nigeria down!”

The wedding wasn’t the only major family update Boyega shared.

During the same interview, he confirmed that his wife is pregnant and that they are expecting a son.

“We got a baby cooking,” he revealed.

Boyega expressed how much his growing family means to him, saying, “My life is completely, completely fulfilled in terms of family. It’s been so nice with the timing.”

The actor also confirmed that he has a young stepson. That detail adds another dimension to his experience with fatherhood, as he is already part of a family raising a child while preparing for another arrival.

While Boyega openly discussed his marriage and children, he did not identify his wife during The Guardian interview.

However, PEOPLE reported on October 13 that speculation has connected him romantically to actress and model Lashontae Heckard.

According to the publication, the two have attracted attention through their social media activity, including Heckard’s Instagram bio, which reportedly reads “Tae Boyega.” PEOPLE also pointed to photographs that appear to reference their relationship.

Still, those clues should not be mistaken for a direct confirmation of her identity as Boyega’s wife. The actor chose not to disclose his spouse’s name in the interview, leaving that part of his private life unaddressed.

Beyond the relationship speculation, Boyega’s comments about becoming a father offered a more personal look at how his priorities have changed.

His family announcement emerged during a conversation about “Damilola: The Untold Story,” a BBC documentary examining the death of his childhood friend Damilola Taylor.

According to The Guardian’s coverage of the documentary, Damilola was just 10 years old when he was fatally attacked in Peckham, South London, on November 27, 2000.

Boyega was eight at the time and was among the last people to see Damilola alive. The tragedy deeply affected his childhood and his understanding of violence, loss, and personal safety.

The documentary, which premiered on BBC Two on October 5, features Boyega and his sister Grace reflecting on their friendship with Damilola and the lasting emotional impact of his death.

That experience also provides important context for Boyega’s current perspective on family.

When discussing the kind of parent he hopes to be, the actor emphasized that his greatest concern is ensuring “I’m present, I’m consistent and full of love.”

For Boyega, that commitment also means reconsidering how much space his acting career occupies in his life.

“I’ve tried to, as much as possible – especially following periods when I’ve worked a lot – to de-centre my career,” he told The Guardian.

“There have been certain moments when I’ve known that this is a time for family. Y’know, there’s stuff to do.”

Boyega’s decision to prioritize his personal life marks an important chapter for an actor whose career has included “Attack the Block,” the “Star Wars” sequel trilogy, “The Woman King,” and “They Cloned Tyrone,” as documented by The Guardian.

His latest revelations also show that he has been building a life outside the entertainment industry’s constant attention, even while continuing to work in film.

With nearly two years of marriage behind him, a stepson already in his life, and another son on the way, Boyega appears focused on protecting the family he has built while remaining present for the moments that matter most.

NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with political strategist and former senior Republican congressional adviser Rina Shah about how President Trump's personal grievances and projects are affecting the chances of GOP candidates in the upcoming election.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Rina Shah has been listening with us. She is a political strategist with experience as a GOP congressional adviser. Good morning, Rina.RINA SHAH: Hi. Good morning.MARTIN: So Mara mentioned the president's complaints, and in some cases, moves against people like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, the media, the government of Norway. Is - does any of that motivate voters at this point, either in his base or independents?SHAH: Well, I think it's really important to see what this really is. The diesel deal and the energy ceasefire announcement, I believe, are less about immediate relief and more about creating a permission structure for Republican candidates. The volumes are really too small to meaningfully move prices before November 3. I think most analysts are saying that plainly, and most of us kind of get that.But the move lets candidates say that the president is trying something on cost instead of doing nothing. And that's really the narrow political utility here. The risk is that Zelenskyy's criticism and then the lack of clear details on the ceasefire turn it into another foreign policy story that down-ballot Republicans then have to explain rather than use.MARTIN: But also it doesn't work. It doesn't seem to be working. He's saying one thing, and the facts prove to be otherwise. And to that end, you know, the president's defending - he's aggressively defended his decision to launch trade wars with much of the world, his military war with Iran. Those are both things that have raised prices for Americans. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll indicates that independent voters favor Democrats by 19 points on the economy. So the question is, you're saying, even if it creates a permission structure, does that - is that enough?SHAH: Well, look, let's look at the broader midterm picture here. Trump is running the same play he always has - make every race about himself and then bet that his base's intensity outweighs his approval numbers, which we know are pretty dismal. The difference this cycle is that the grievances that are driving a lot of the White House's agenda - which are media fights, the Department of Justice's action against people from the first term, his personal score-settling - those are more self-generated than they were in 2016 or '18. Back then, a larger share of what he amplified tracked the existing voter frustration.Now more of it originates from inside the administration, and it's getting projected outward, and that really changes the utility for candidates. It motivates the core base, but it doesn't give swing voters a new reason to show up when their main concern is still the price of diesel and groceries. But I'd be remiss if I didn't mention here the practical problem for Republicans in these next three weeks, and it's that there is not a clean off-ramp for them. Candidates in really tight races would prefer a more narrow message on things like border enforcement and costs, and the White House is not structured at all to deliver that.Trump treats the midterms as an extension of his own presidency rather than a set of local races, which is really unusual, even by our modern standards. Presidents have always campaigned, but they have rarely, rarely made themselves the constant central character this late while the party is trailing on the economy. And what that does is forces candidates to either fully nationalize their races or spend time creating distance, and neither of which is ideal with three weeks left.MARTIN: Sure. So if the president can't or won't focus his message on what voters care about right now, and if there doesn't seem to be anybody in the president's circle who can get him to do that, is there anything that congressional candidates can do?SHAH: Oh, that is the question du jour. Look, three weeks out, it's very hard for anyone to redirect him. He sets the agenda. The people closest to him can sometimes influence timing or emphasis on a particular issue like prices, but they rarely change his overall focus or stop him from going where he wants to go. At this point in the midterm cycle, I think the political reality of the map and the polls can sometimes force a more narrow message. But that's really different, again, from someone inside Trump world circle - they're successfully shifting him.I would say this - look, if the polls are right and Republicans are trailing on the broad economy or the cost-of-living question, the other issues that can still drive their turnout are the border and public safety. Those have consistently been stronger for Republicans in recent cycles, and they give candidates a concrete contrast - things like enforcement, resources and results, versus what they argue has been a more permissive Democratic policy.MARTIN: OK, before we let you go through...SHAH: Also energy domestic production.MARTIN: Thirty seconds left, though. Republicans...SHAH: SureMARTIN: ...A big campaign bank. Republicans are outspending Democrats in these final weeks. Do they have - is that enough to erase some of these Democratic advantages that we're seeing in the polls?SHAH: Truly, I don't believe so. I think right now, what we're looking at is a real downside because what's emanating from the White House has created that. The downside here to Trump's strategy so far is that it's locked the midterms into a pure referendum on him. And look, by inserting himself constantly and tying every race to his record and grievances, he's made it really hard for vulnerable Republicans to run as independent of Washington. And in a cycle where his approval is low and prices remain high, that nationalizes races in a way that often favors the out-party...MARTIN: OK.SHAH: ...Which is the Democrats.MARTIN: That is Republican political strategist Rina Shah. Rina, thanks.SHAH: Thank you.

Lithuania’s prime minister on Monday described the recently announced diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin as “shameful” and “disgraceful,” also questioning whether a written agreement exists.

Speaking to Sky News on the sidelines of Poland’s Warsaw Security Forum, Mindaugas Sinkevicius said he had seen social media posts about the arrangement but no written deal.

“We’re not proud of it. It’s shameful, disgraceful,” he said. “I’m not sure if it’s even underway or if it’s just a political claim. I’ve not seen any deal, written deal, I’ve just seen the tweets … not the deal actually.”

Asked whether Trump could still be trusted amid concerns over his approach to Putin, the premier replied: “Well, I hope so, I hope so.”

Sinkevicius also urged Europe to strengthen its ability to act independently.

Asked whether Europe should “go it alone,” he said European countries need to “do as much as we can” and “count on ourselves.”

At the same time, he stressed the enduring nature of ties despite changes in political leadership.

“Administrations and politicians change, the bonds remain.”

Trump has blamed rising fuel prices – a key issue in the looming Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections – on the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the ongoing conflict involving Iran.

On Friday, Trump announced a deal under which Moscow agreed to provide fuel to the US and global markets.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal as a “gift” to Putin, warning that easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance Moscow’s war effort.

By Anna Levy

According to recent research: very.

Research conducted by the Movember Institute of Men's Health found that 68 per cent of young Australian men aged 16-25 engaged with masculinity influencers. That’s more than in the UK (61 per cent) or the US (60 per cent).

A 2024 Dublin City University study found that it took roughly 23 minutes of video watching on either TikTok or YouTube Shorts for the algorithms to start recommending "toxic" content.

Another 2024 study by YouGov and girls' empowerment charity Tomorrow Woman found that 42 per cent of female students said their male peers were influenced by the likes of Andrew Tate and the manosphere.

It also found that one in four female high school students in Australia felt unsafe at school due to these behaviours.

Key Event

By Georgia Hitch

Earlier this year, the federal government announced it would introduce laws requiring social media companies give users the option to opt in or out of the algorithm on their feeds.

What does this have to do with the manosphere?

Well, advocates like Chanel Contos argue the algorithm exposes young people to misogynistic content and fuels the prevalence of sexual violence and gendered attitudes towards women.

We asked Chanel what regular Australians should know about the campaign and legislation.

"Social media algorithms are increasingly flooding young men's feeds with radical misogynistic content. This is inciting and worsening real-world harm, particularly towards women and girls. The content they're systematically targeted with frequently blames women for any misfortunes they experience, and reinstates harmful and outdated gender stereotypes, like that women shouldn’t hold jobs or earn their own money.

"Fifteen thousand Australians signed our open letter to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and in early September the Government committed to the #FixOurFeeds campaign as part of the Digital Duty of Care legislation — you may have heard it referred to as 'My Feed, My Way'.

"This commitment to allow Australians to turn their algorithms on and off will give people control back over their own data and feeds and disrupt how easily recommendation algorithm systems feed young men and boys manosphere content. The legislation is expected to be introduced into parliament this week, and we're focused on ensuring the detail matches the ambition."

By Georgia Hitch

A new ABC documentary looking into the manosphere, The State of Man, airs tonight, and its host, Marc Fennell, shared how he approached the series.

"No matter who I’m talking to, whether I personally agree with them or not, I like to give people enough space to eventually say the quiet part out loud," he said.

"There’s a version of documentary making where you create big confrontations or stunts because they make great television. Sometimes people just shit stir. And look, I love watching that stuff. But it’s not really what I do.

"I try to approach people with clear eyes and a critical mind, but also genuine curiosity. I’m not sitting there waiting to catch somebody out. I actually want to know why they think what they think.

"The strange thing is that when you give people that space, sometimes you hear some truly cooked things."

You can watch The State of Man tonight at 8pm on ABC TV, or add it to your watchlist and stream it for free on ABC iview.

By Georgia Hitch

We're lucky enough to be joined by three experts today to cover a few different areas linked to the manosphere.

Dr Billy Garvey is a developmental paediatrician, researcher and author. He is the founder of Guiding Growing Minds, a social enterprise bringing evidence-based child development science to communities and families across Australia. He's also the co-host of the Pop Culture Parenting podcast.

Genevieve Sheppard  is a former teacher and currently holds the position of principal advisor, respectful relationships education at Our Watch. For over a decade, she has supported governments, education systems and schools to embed evidence-based, whole-of-school approaches to preventing gender-based violence.

Dr Zac Seidler is a clinical psychologist and leading researcher in men's mental health. He is the global director of men's health research at the Movember Institute of Men's Health, leading research focused on how masculinity, culture and social norms influence men's mental health and help-seeking behaviours.

The Department of Homeland Security released a statement Monday detailing what they said happened over the weekend during an incident in which federal agents used tear gas on protesters in Salem.

On Saturday, Oct. 10, the Salem Police Department said it received reports of a large group of people blocking Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles near the intersection of Lancaster Drive and Sunnyview Road. Police said they also received reports that federal agents had used tear gas to clear the crowd. Following the incident, several 911 calls were made from people who reported eye irritation and trouble breathing.

According to DHS, federal agents were surrounded by “anti-ICE agitators” on Saturday morning. DHS said protestors on foot and in vehicles blocked federal agents from leaving the area.

“These rioters struck government vehicles with baseball bats and rocks, threatening harm to our officers and the public while causing significant damage,” said DHS in a statement to OPB. “Officers relied on their training to control the situation with professionalism and integrity.”

In their statement, DHS said violence against their agents or any law enforcement official will not be tolerated.

“Our officers carry out their Congressionally mandated duties in service to public safety and the rule of law. Any bystander or individual who assaults, obstructs, or violently attacks officers will be subject to arrest and prosecution permitted by law.”

The agency also said its officers are trained in de-escalation tactics and will use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations.

Salem police said it had no prior knowledge of ICE’s activity and does not coordinate with ICE operations. The incident remains under investigation.

A fugitive accused of getting rich off programs meant to help Venezuelans is now in U.S. custody, facing charges in a sprawling corruption scandal tied to Nicolás Maduro’s regime.

Alvaro Pulido Vargas, 62, was arrested during a Homeland Security Task Force operation and is scheduled to appear Tuesday, Oct. 13, in federal court in South Florida, the Justice Department announced.

The Colombian national faces two criminal cases alleging he helped funnel money from Venezuelan government bribery schemes through U.S. banks to hide illicit profits.

A reward poster for Alvaro Pulido Vargas is marked "In Custody" following his arrest. Federal prosecutors accuse him of money laundering tied to Venezuelan government bribery schemes. (United States Attorney’s Office — Southern District of Florida)

"Pulido is charged in two separate, significant money laundering schemes, both using the U.S. financial system to hide the profits from his bribery and greed off the backs of the Venezuelan people," said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the arrest Sunday on X, accusing Pulido Vargas of exploiting programs meant to provide essential supplies and housing.

"His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it," Blanche wrote.

Pulido Vargas, also known as German Enrique Rubio Salas, was charged in 2019 and again in 2021. The Justice Department said he previously was convicted of drug trafficking in Italy in 1997 under that alias.

"For years, DEA and our HSTF partners have pursued Pulido Vargas across borders. Today, that pursuit has brought him to the Southern District of Florida," DEA Administrator Terrance Cole said.

The newer case centers on approximately $1.6 billion in Venezuelan government contracts to supply food and medicine through CLAP, a government-run distribution program.

His son, Emmanuel Enrique Rubio Gonzalez, and former Venezuelan state Governor Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora were among four others charged in the case.

Approximately $180 million moved through or into the United States, including accounts in South Florida, according to prosecutors.

A wisp of smoke on a cloudless early August morning was one of the first indications that a wildfire had started in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of northern New Mexico. Lightning struck near the village of Cundiyó, and a blaze quickly erupted in the drought-stricken canyons surrounding the Río Frijoles.



Both this 13-mile stream and the Río en Media descend from the Sangres and flow into Santa Cruz Lake, a reservoir that releases their water into the Santa Cruz River, which is then joined by another tributary, the Río Quemado.



Like the spurs of a railway, some 30 hand-dug channels, or acequias, deliver that water — collectively owned by around 3,000 parciantes or members — to the small family farms of several historic communities. These acequias — established hundreds of years ago and maintained to this day — predate the dam by many generations and are themselves recognized as political subdivisions of New Mexico, overseen by commissions and individual mayordomos who steward their distribution and maintenance.

But with more than half of the Río Frijoles in the direct path of the fire, the health of the watershed — and the future of the area’s irrigation — were at risk.



“Once it started, I was just waiting for a call, a text, a message from somebody to see if they could pump water” from the lake, said Ron Gallegos, chair of the Santa Cruz Irrigation District, which manages the water for local irrigators downstream.



“And sure enough, they did.”



Within days, U.S. Forest Service aircraft began scooping up lake water to douse the fire and spraying slurry to slow its spread. Gallegos received a contract from the agency to pay the Irrigation District one cent for every gallon it used. It wasn’t much — about $8,500 for about 850,000 gallons, a comparatively small amount of water — but trying to save the watershed, which serves the small farms of some 3,000 people, made it seem worthwhile, Gallegos said.

As of early October, almost two months after the Frijoles Fire ignited, it’s about 90% contained. An initial assessment showed that most of the fire burned at a low intensity, potentially minimizing the post-fire impacts. But flooding could still lead to a rise in sediment, creating turbidity in the lake, and local communities are concerned about the effects that this sediment and the fire retardant might have on the quality of the water on which they depend.



EVEN BEFORE THE FRIJOLES FIRE, the rapid shifts in extreme weather between drought and torrential rains in recent years had made irrigation here precarious. This year, with little snow and high temperatures, runoff has been severely curtailed. “It could be the worst on record,” said Steve Finch, a hydrogeologist and geochemist at an Albuquerque-based firm. A nearby U.S. Geological Survey gauge registered about 4 cubic feet per second all summer long. “Normally, it should be 20 or 30,” he said.



The low levels of warmer water spurred an algae bloom earlier this year that turned the lake a murky green and infused it with a strong putrid scent.



Joel Esquibel operates and maintains the dam just as his father did before him. Several times a week, he climbs a concrete buttress to the top of the dam to observe the height of the lake’s water. As the fire burned, his concern increased. “The only time it was lower was when it was dredged” in the late 1980s, he said. By the end of September, however, a moisture plume from Hurricane Polo had brought the lake up 15 feet.



But too much water has its own risks. In 2025, a historic flood destroyed acequia infrastructure, and the damage brought irrigation to a halt as small communities rebuilt headgates and cleared out debris and silt, a process that took months and cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.



This September’s historic rains flushed Frijoles Fire debris and silt into the lake, and Finch worries that this will reduce the reservoir’s capacity. He estimates that over the past 100 years, Santa Cruz Lake has already accumulated 1,000 acre-feet of silt, or about one-quarter of its capacity. He doesn’t know yet how much silt the post-fire rains have brought, but he said that reservoir will have to be dredged again one day to “refurbish its storage capacity.” 



ON AUG. 4, the day the fire started, New Mexico Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D, requested that the Government Accountability Office, a federal watchdog agency, “examine the prevalence and potential effects of toxic metals in fire retardants” used by the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior. The letter — which emphasized the “essential, lifesaving support” of aerial firefighting and was signed by eight congresspeople — added that “recent reports have raised questions about the safety of fire retardants commonly used by aerial firefighters.”



Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-N.M.) requested an examination of the potential effects of toxic metals in fire retardants. Credit: AP Photo/Francis Chung

“All fire retardants used by the Forest Service fall into the Environmental Protection Agency’s ‘practically non-toxic’ category for mammals, including humans, and aquatic species,” Forest Service spokesperson Claudia Brookshire wrote in an email to High Country News. “The Forest Service prohibits retardant drops within waterways and within mapped avoidance areas for cultural resources, or threatened, endangered, proposed, candidate or sensitive species.”



While fire retardants largely comprise two forms of phosphate widely used in fertilizers, investigations in California revealed arsenic, cadmium, chromium and lead in samples collected after the Palisades, Eaton and Franklin fires.

Three years after the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire ripped through 340,000 acres of forest lands in northern New Mexico, independent analysis showed the presence of heavy metals in private well water. A 2026 report attributed it to natural ores as well as burnt structures and fire suppressants.



According to the Forest Service, some 453,000 gallons of retardant were dropped on the Frijoles Fire, more than a quarter of the 1,600,000 gallons used on the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire. But the Frijoles Fire is significantly smaller: At 16,000 acres, it’s less than 5% of the size of the Hermit’s Peak blaze.



Asked at a public meeting in early September in the nearby village of Truchas whether there were heavy metals present in the fire retardant used on the Frijoles Fire, Lawrence Lujan, a deputy district ranger for the Santa Fe National Forest, referred High Country News to the manufacturer.



“No heavy metals are added to any PHOS-CHEK fire retardant formulations; any trace amounts of heavy metals present are naturally occurring within the raw materials used to formulate the solution,” wrote Zak Bollenbacher, president of the Americas Retardants business at Perimeter Solutions, the retardant’s manufacturer, in an email. The phosphate in the retardant used in the Frijoles Fire, he added, undergoes multiple processes to remove “heavy metal levels below fertilizer grade.”



PHOS-CHEK IS A BRAND of firefighting foam sprayed from aircraft to prevent wildfires from spreading. It was developed in the late 1960s by industrial giant Monsanto. While most of its  ingredients were made public in material safety data sheets, a small percentage remain undisclosed as trade secrets. This prompted a team of researchers from University of Southern California to investigate the presence of heavy metals in retardants using data from fires that occurred between 2009 and 2021.



The team looked at 14 types, three of them in the Phos-Chek line, that are now owned by Perimeter Solutions. The results published in 2024 show that one Phos-Chek product, Phos-Chek LC95-W — once considered the world’s most widely used retardant — contains levels of heavy metals orders of magnitude higher than the EPA’s drinking water standards. The Forest Service phased out the product in 2024, but the agency confirmed that it had used this type as well as the two others on the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon blaze. Another retardant used on Hermit’s Peak and, according to Bollenbacher, used “to help contain the Frijoles Fire” was also used in the recent major California fires. Later analysis by the USC team revealed high levels of heavy metals.



According to lead researcher Daniel McCurry, the USC team did not analyze the second type of retardant used on the Frijoles Fire, a variety called Phos-Chek 259-Fx, because it lacked access to all of the manufacturer’s samples.



On the ground, acequia parciantes are holding their breath. The entire lake has darkened to the color of ash, and concerns about water quality remain. No more water releases are planned for the rest of the year, Finch said, so whatever debris and silt ended up in the lake will have time to settle over the winter months. That means that the debris is unlikely to get distributed into the acequias. At least, not this year.

aiden-buzzetti-china-data-centers:
America is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build data centers in an attempt to lead the development of new artificial intelligence technology. Both lobbyists and lawmakers argue constantly about who could or should make the chips inside them, but there are far fewer people who ask about the components that connect those chips to each other and the outside world. That’s a big mistake because many of those components are made in China.

Optical transceivers are a major part of data center infrastructure, enabling high-speed data transfer between servers, racks and facilities. Nearly every major AI cluster in the country depends on them to operate, and China is the main supplier. In fact, Johns Hopkins Associate Professor Yury Dvorkin recently told Breitbart that China supplies approximately two-thirds of global optical transceivers.

Chinese companies such as Innolight, which got added to the Department of War’s Chinese Military Companies list this year, and Eoptolink are among the leading suppliers. Would any serious country allow an adversary to dominate an industry on which it is increasingly reliant?

None of this is accidental. China’s strategy is well documented: rely on state money and industrial policy to research critical technologies; undercut foreign competition; and, when they’ve taken the market, use it for leverage. This has happened for years in industries from solar panels to batteries – which means we should’ve learned this lesson already.

Rural carriers across America bought cheap Huawei and ZTE equipment for years. When Congress finally woke up to the threat, they had to allocate $5 billion in taxpayer funds to rip it out and replace it, which still hasn’t been finished. We could make the same mistake again; and this time, the scale and stakes are far larger.

Chinese companies have also been getting better at avoiding the rules we already have and are increasingly routing goods through third countries to avoid tariffs. The White House itself has estimated that transshipment strategies have resulted in a $19 to $26 billion loss.

But now, Washington is moving. Over the summer, it was reported that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is poised to move quickly to ban Chinese optical transceivers imports to protect our AI infrastructure. Chairman Brendan Carr and his team have shown that they take national security seriously and should follow through. More recently, bipartisan legislation was introduced in the Senate to keep Chinese optical transceivers out of the federal government’s most sensitive national security systems. While good, these efforts are receiving pushback from industry.

Major companies and associations representing the biggest names in tech have advocated against proposed actions. Yet an open letter signed by some of those companies warned of the need for a more secure digital ecosystem in the AI era. If security really is a topic of concern, they should care about data center components and AI infrastructure.

An AI model is only as secure as the hardware it runs on, and you can’t build an AI stack that is trustworthy on a foundation supplied by companies bound by the Chinese government. If Big Tech really cared about security, they would recognize that the physical infrastructure in data centers has to be part of that equation.

Theodore Roosevelt understood that a nation that can’t secure its own industrial base cannot truly govern itself. The AI race will be won or lost on infrastructure, and that means optical transceivers matter just as much as chips. To keep America safe, the FCC should finalize its ban, Congress should pass a bill, and technology companies should stop lobbying to support Chinese hardware.

We already paid once to rip out Huawei. We shouldn’t have to again.

Aiden Buzzetti is the President of the Bull Moose Project.

Business

Less than a week after Mesabi said it would build a steel mill there, Iowa legislators gave it a $1.4 billion tax break.

By Evan Ramstad

Until two weeks ago, I thought the closest Iowa had come to having a steel industry was when the University of Iowa’s football coach in 1979 got permission to copy the uniform of the Pittsburgh Steelers.

I didn’t know my home state’s legislature in the mid-1990s put together a $75 million incentive package to attract a Canadian company called IPSCO to build a small mill along the eastern border that would melt scrap into heavy steel plates.

Now part of a Swedish firm called SSAB, that mill near Muscatine, Iowa, continues to make steel for highway bridges and the towering windmills that dot the prairie.

But when it comes to getting a deal with Iowa’s lawmakers, Mesabi Metallics of Nashwauk, Minn., just put that business and every other one to shame.

On Monday, Sept. 28, Mesabi Metallics announced from the White House that it would build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. Just four days later, Iowa legislators agreed to give the company nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks to do it.

Iowans will wind up paying for this corporate giveaway for at least a decade, as the subsidies equate to about $820,000 for each of the 1,750 full-time workers Mesabi plans to hire there.

That’s their right, of course. Minnesota has been down this road with Mesabi and its India-based parent Essar Group many times to help get its new Nashwauk mine going.

But with this deal, Iowans thrust the arms race of states chasing businesses onto a higher plane. Minnesota and other Midwestern states may have to pony up more as businesses seek tax breaks that begin where Iowa left off.

This deal is more than twice as large as Minnesota’s biggest economic development initiative, the Destination Medical Center project in Rochester that involved about $585 million in state and local funds over 20 years. That project helped Minnesota’s largest private employer, Mayo Clinic, which is investing more than $5 billion over that period.

Now Iowa has shown it’s willing to spend far more taxpayer money, in an even shorter time, to assist a business that employs a fraction of the 57,000 workers Mayo does in Minnesota.

“The ceiling now becomes the floor,” Dan Dawson, the Republican who chairs the Iowa Senate Ways and Means Committee, told his colleagues on Oct. 2 when he voted against the incentive package for Mesabi Metallics.

“I, in good conscience, cannot support giving to any single corporation and their financiers ... what simply amounts to the largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa’s history,” Dawson added. “I choose conservatism, not corporatism.”

It’s no wonder Dawson could sniff out a bad deal. In his regular job, he’s a special agent in charge at the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation in Council Bluffs.

Election-year politics is at work in this whole affair, of course. President Donald Trump himself became the first person to announce the steel mill, and the federal government’s Export-Import Bank is providing a $770 million loan to Essar. At Trump’s side were Iowa’s outgoing Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, and members of the state’s congressional delegation.

Trump and Reynolds hope the news will give a last-minute boost to Republicans in Iowa, including U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is in a tight race with Democrat Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Joni Ernst.

The project seemed to come out of nowhere. Only a week before the White House announcement, the Des Moines Register reported an unidentified company had approached landowners in Lee County, Iowa, a bit south on the Mississippi from Muscatine, for property rumored to be for a steel mill.

Mesabi only just started production at the Nashwauk mine on Sept. 17. Company executives were telling the media at the ribbon-cutting that they planned to ship the ore to mills in Louisiana.

As Dawson and other Iowa legislators made clear during the one-day special session, Mesabi was apparently pitting Iowa against Arkansas for a steel mill.

Arkansas has several large steel mills, including ones owned by industry leaders Nucor and U.S. Steel. However, Dawson said state officials in Arkansas told him they were concerned about Mesabi’s and Essar’s abilities to pay for a mill. Yet Iowa’s Gov. Reynolds pushed aside the state’s economic development agency to get a deal done quickly.

“It’s my belief she negotiated against herself, because Arkansas, I do not believe, was ever actually at the table seriously,” Dawson said. “And by negotiating against herself, she negotiated against the Iowa taxpayer.”

And Reynolds offered the company something particularly sweet: the option to transfer Iowa’s tax credits to other companies, meaning Mesabi can make money from them or use them to raise capital.

As one of the slowest-growing regions in the nation, the Midwest is vulnerable to companies like Mesabi that have big projects and bigger appetites to be rewarded for them.

“Incentives are supposed to make a good deal better, not a bad deal good,” Dawson said just before the Iowa Senate voted 28-19 in favor of Mesabi’s deal.

I have often criticized Minnesota’s Democrats for sharp increases in state spending they engineered in 2023 and 2025. But in Iowa today, it’s Republicans with a trifecta in the Legislature and governor’s office playing loose with taxes and taxpayers.

Back here in Minnesota, GOP party members criticized Gov. Tim Walz for not attracting the mill to our state. So with the election around the corner, I have to wonder: If Minnesota’s Republicans get more power, will they hand out tax breaks to companies like Mesabi with the gusto Iowa’s just did?

Because if so, they have lost their way. So many Republicans have in the Trump era.

Noah McFadyen completed an impressive debut for South Australia, taking a return catch as his side beat Victoria. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

South Australia's campaign for a third-straight Sheffield Shield title is off to a winning start with victory over Victoria.

The Redbacks won by an innings and 40 runs at Junction Oval.

Debutant Noah McFadyen, who scored a century in SA's only innings of 508, took the final wicket with a caught-and-bowled to clinch the win.

South Australia has started its Sheffield Shield campaign in the same way it ended the last one, beating Victoria at Junction Oval.

The two-time defending champions wrapped up their dominating start today, beating the home side by an innings and 40 runs.

Fittingly, debutant Noah McFadyen took the last wicket of the game when he had David Moody caught and bowled, after top-scoring with 134 in SA's innings.

McFadyen had hit two sixes to go from 88 to 100, finished with 16 fours and five maximums.

The 23-year-old all-rounder had match figures of 3-65, including Moody's wicket to clinch the game.

Resuming at 7-175 and needing another 89 to bat again, Victoria was dismissed for 224.

Victoria made 244 in its first innings and SA took the game away from them with 508.

Fergus O'Neill top-scored in Victoria's second innings with 62, while Nathan McAndrew and Henry Thornton took three wickets apiece.

met-lee-krasner-jackson-pollock:
Anastasia Tsioulcas

When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981.
                
                    
                    Ernst Haas/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

There's a new blockbuster show at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Past Continuous features two artists: Jackson Pollock, with many of his instantly recognizable "drip" paintings, and Lee Krasner, an artist often overshadowed by Pollock, who was her husband. But in this major exhibition, Krasner is finally getting her due — and on her own terms.

This gargantuan show is replete with Pollock's greatest hits, the giant, frozen dances of paint splashed on canvas that have become iconic. But this exhibition of more than 120 works (74 from Krasner, and 48 from Pollock) reveals Krasner as an Abstract Expressionist titan, too.

One of the first works that catches your eye is a 1955 Krasner collage.

"Collage was very catalytic for her at these crucial moments in her life," said Brinda Kumar, one of the two Met curators who put together this exhibition. "She was literally sometimes tearing up older bodies of work to create a new chapter."

This work is 1955's Bald Eagle, a riotous mix of browns, blacks, fuchsia, and orange, with a claw-like slash of yellow. And right in the middle is a cutout whose shape evokes the head of a bald eagle — and that's the name that Krasner gave to this collage.

Lee Krasner, Bald Eagle, 1955, Oil, paper, and canvas collage on linen,  ASOM Collection
                
                    
                    2026 Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
                    
                
                hide caption

Pollock's rejects were the source material for Bald Eagle, according to Kumar. "Krasner has very intentionally and deliberately cut up discarded Pollock works from this era in the 1950s, where you can see his distinctive drip still evident," she said.

When you put Krasner's collages next to Pollock's drip paintings, we see something new in the juxtaposition, said another Met curator, David Breslin.

"But that doesn't mean that the individual parts forgo their histories or their pasts," Breslin said. "We see that almost as a metaphor for couples in relationships as well. You form a unit, yet you also have all the things in your head, in your mind, in your heart that are your own, that don't change."

And sure enough, just past these collages, a visitor will see one of Pollock's classic drip paintings — 1952's Convergence, with neon orange and electric yellow so bright and bold that they foreshadow 1980s subway graffiti. The curators have put Convergence on a freestanding wall near windows, with daylight shining through — evoking the energy of a contemporary gallery.

Installation view of Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, on view at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Oct. 4, 2026 – Jan. 31, 2027.
                
                    
                    Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met
                    
                
                hide caption

The unspoken challenge of this show is to invite comparisons between wife-and-husband artists. In popular imagination, Pollock is often the troubled genius and hero, and Krasner is sidelined as a helpmate. She knew what people thought — but she didn't care.

In a 1978 interview on a television program called Inside New York's Art World, the interviewer asked Krasner what she was doing while Pollock was becoming so famous.

"I was working all the time," Krasner replied. "I doubt our relationship could have existed at all if I weren't working. In terms of what other people think, I can't do anything about that. You know, that's not my preoccupation anyway. As long as I was able to work, I went about my business."

That's true, but Krasner was also very savvy about her market value as a female artist, said curator Brinda Kumar.

Lee Krasner, Mosaic Table, 1947 Mosaic of mixed media (including broken glass, keys, coins, ceramic, and pebbles) in cement; iron wagon-wheel armature with steel
                
                    
                    Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met
                    
                
                hide caption

"She was very cognizant of the gender dynamics and the gender politics. His career was the one that was more successful at the time."

To that end, she made certain calculations. They made their home in Springs, N.Y., a small fishing community on the far side of Long Island — a location Krasner chose specifically to get Pollock away from the business and booze of Manhattan. Pollock used a barn on the property to work on his enormous canvases, while Krasner painted first in the kitchen and then in a small, upstairs bedroom.

Lee Krasner was all about reinvention — both artistic and personal. Born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn, she was the child of Orthodox Jewish parents who came from a shtetl in what is now Ukraine. Nobody in her family knew anything about art.

She gave herself a series of new names: first Lenore, then Lee Krasner. She sculpted a new life as a young, bold artist. And she became a quintessential networker who knew everybody in New York's art scene.

Journalist Mary Gabriel has written extensively about Krasner, including in her 2018 book Ninth Street Women: Lee Krasner, Elaine de Kooning, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler: Five Painters and the Movement that Changed Modern Art. Gabriel says that unlike her husband, Krasner kept reinventing her style.

"Krasner was so fascinating because she changed, not even by the decade. Every few years, she tries something new," Gabriel said. "She was always searching, which in a way is the most, I think, honest way to be an artist, because art is about discovery."

These include what Krasner called her "Little Images" — densely populated paintings from the late 1940s of nearly hieroglyphic looking symbols, all jostling for space on small canvases — as well as immense works she created, especially after Pollock died in a car crash in 1956. Pollock was plagued by alcoholism and depression, and he cheated on her; his girlfriend of the time was one of the passengers in the crash.

Krasner continued to be financially savvy as well. After Pollock's death, she more than tripled the price of one of his most famous works, Autumn Rhythm (Number 30), to sell it to the Met — a sum that not just set the pace for Pollock's market value, but for a tide of modern artists.

For this show, Autumn Rhythm was moved off its traditional museum wall to a freestanding display, Kumar noted.

"It is almost architectural in a way, because it's set against this slate grey color," she said. "The swirling blacks get animated in a whole new way, and the familiar teals and the familiar whites surge with a new energy."

Krasner seized upon her own new energy in the years after Pollock's death. She took over the barn studio that had been her husband's — and made giant, joyful work, brimming with life and lushness, as curator David Breslin noted.

Lee Krasner, The Seasons, 1957, Oil and house paint on canvas, Whitney Museum of American Art
                
                    
                    The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
                    
                
                hide caption

"You see this incredible painting that's almost 17 feet wide called The Seasons, that has these forms and bodies, eyes and body parts and these things that look like vegetation sprawling out of it," Breslin said. "So she makes, almost in a contradictory way, some of the brightest, most vibrant paintings the year after his death."

And in some way, this whole show is all about Lee Krasner finally being able to claim her own space. Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous runs at the Met until Jan. 31.
